Reminder cancellation on reschedule is fire-and-forget

The try/catch wraps a `forEach` whose callback returns a promise that is never awaited. Any rejection from `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` will not be caught and the mutation continues. Errors are lost, and on the `immediateDelete=true` email path the DB row is never updated, so if the SendGrid cancel fails, the system has no record that cancellation was attempted.

Reminder cancellation in requestReschedule is fire-and-forget

`bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited. The trpc mutation then proceeds to send emails, update DB, delete refs, etc., and finally returns before the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation has completed (or even started). Failures are not propagated. Should be a `for...of` loop with `await`, or collect and `Promise.all`.

Reminder cancellation in workflow delete is fire-and-forget

`scheduledReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited before `ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` runs. The workflow delete cascades through `WorkflowStep` and may delete the `WorkflowReminder` rows (via onDelete: Cascade) before SendGrid/Twilio cancellation completes, leaving third-party systems with still-scheduled sends and no DB record to retry. Await the cancellations before deleting the workflow.

Reminder cancellation for disabled event types is fire-and-forget

The `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` block calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting. These are then followed by further awaits like `prisma.workflowsOnEventTypes.deleteMany`, so the mutation returns before cancellations complete and any error is silently swallowed.

Reminder cancellation on step edit is fire-and-forget

`remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => {...})` does not await. The mutation continues and returns while SendGrid/Twilio cancellations may still be in flight. Errors are silently swallowed. Await the operations.

unscheduledReminders query ignores the new cancelled flag

The query that picks up `scheduled: false` reminders to push to SendGrid does not filter on `cancelled`. When a booking is cancelled more than 72 hours before a reminder fires, the reminder row has `cancelled: true` but `scheduled: false`. The next CRON run within 72h of `scheduledDate` will still schedule it via SendGrid. The CRON will subsequently try to cancel the resulting SendGrid send in its 1-hour window, but this is wasteful at best and creates a window in which the email is queued. Add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `cancelled: false`) to the `where` filter on line 82-87.

Cancel loop awaits SendGrid calls sequentially

Inside `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` each iteration awaits a SendGrid HTTP call before moving on. With any non-trivial number of cancellations this serialises the network round-trips (CRON has a hard 15-min cadence and other tenants share it). Use `Promise.allSettled` (or chunked parallel batches) so a single failed call doesn't abort the others and so throughput is reasonable.

1-hour cancel window leaves reminders scheduled in SendGrid

`remindersToCancel` only matches `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Reminders that were already pushed to SendGrid and whose `scheduledDate` is between 1 and 72 hours away are silently skipped: they remain as pending sends in SendGrid. If the CRON is delayed beyond the 1-hour buffer (which it can be, given that it runs every 15 minutes and can be throttled), SendGrid will deliver a reminder for a booking that was cancelled or rescheduled — the same bug this PR is meant to fix. Either cancel in SendGrid immediately on the cancel/reschedule path, or process all `cancelled: true` reminders in this loop, not just the next hour.

Signature change of deleteScheduledEmailReminder is inconsistent across the codebase

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` now requires a `reminderId: number` as the first parameter. Existing callers were updated, but the parameter order (id before referenceId) is unusual since the function historically only needed the external reference. Consider reordering to `(referenceId, reminderId, immediateDelete)` to match `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`'s spirit (which keeps referenceId first) and to minimise future misuse.

SMS cancellation deletes the DB row even when Twilio cancel fails

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` first calls `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and then unconditionally deletes the DB row, all inside the same `try`. If Twilio throws, the catch logs and returns, but the SMS may still be queued at Twilio and there is no record to retry. The flow for email intentionally defers cancellation to a CRON-style mechanism for resilience; the SMS path has no equivalent. Either mirror the email design (`cancelled: true` + CRON) or move the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` outside the try so the delete only happens on Twilio success.

Verification-code TextField is not bound to form state

In the phone-number verification UI, `TextField` for the verification code uses a local `verificationCode` state via `onChange`, but is rendered with `value={verificationCode}` and no `name` registration. The field shows correctly while mounted, but loses its value if the component remounts (e.g. switching action types triggers `setNumberVerified(false)` and `setIsPhoneNumberNeeded(...)` re-renders). It also leaks `verificationCode` between steps because it is component-level state, not scoped to `step.stepNumber`. The original layout (before this PR's refactor) had the same code, but since the panel was hoisted into its own block here, multiple steps now share the same single state variable.

Step-deletion cancellations are fire-and-forget before prisma.workflowStep.delete

`remindersFromStep.forEach(reminder => deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...))` is not awaited before `prisma.workflowStep.delete({ where: { id: oldStep.id } })`. Because `WorkflowStep` has `onDelete: Cascade` on `WorkflowReminder`, the delete will remove the reminder rows from the DB before SendGrid/Twilio has had a chance to cancel them, leaving third-party queues with pending sends. Await the cancellations first.

Past-reminder cleanup deletes rows before SendGrid actually fires

The first action of the CRON deletes every `WorkflowReminder` row whose `scheduledDate <= now`. This is supposed to be housekeeping for already-sent reminders, but the only signal that an email was actually delivered is the row's existence. If SendGrid is delayed or the CRON runs late, reminders that have not been sent yet can be deleted from the DB while still being queued in SendGrid, leading to silent drops. Track delivery status (or only delete `cancelled: true` past reminders) rather than every past-scheduled row.

No tests added for the cancellation fix

This PR changes the data flow for cancelling workflow reminders on booking cancel/reschedule and adds a new DB column plus a new CRON path. There are no tests covering: (a) that `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` sets `cancelled: true` correctly, (b) that the CRON only processes `cancelled: true` rows within the window, (c) that reschedule/reschedule-via-trpc paths actually cancel, or (d) regression coverage for the bug in #7225. The previous attempt also broke things; without tests the same risk exists here.

Existing attendees are allowed to add arbitrary guests

A retry will then hit `uniqueGuests.length === 0` and return a misleading `emails_must_be_unique_valid` error, leaving the meeting with attendees in the DB but not on the calendar and not notified. `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` uses the currently authenticated user's spread and credentials. The booking's actual organizer is loaded into `organizer` but its credentials are not used. When the caller is a team admin or (in the corrected logic) an attendee, the calendar invite will be pushed through whichever calendar integration the caller has, not the organizer's. That causes the organizer to lose control of the event on their primary calendar and may fail entirely if the caller has no calendar credentials for the destinationCalendar.

No upper bound on guests array: trivially exploitable DoS / cost amplification

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max(...)`. A single authed user can submit an array of thousands of valid emails. The handler then performs N inserts, N `getTranslation` calls, one big `Promise.all` of N emails, and a calendar update with an attendees list of size N. There is no per-user / per-booking throttle. A reasonable bound (e.g. `.max(50)` or `.max(100)`) should be enforced at the schema layer to prevent abuse and keep the email/calendar blast radius small.

findFirst -> filter -> update pattern has a TOCTOU race that can create duplicate attendees

The handler reads `booking.attendees` and then issues `prisma.booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`. Between those two statements another request from the same organizer can insert the same guest; because there is no unique index on (bookingId, email) and no transactional check, both requests will succeed and produce duplicate attendee rows that share the same email on the same booking. The de-duplication should be done inside a single transaction (or use a unique constraint) to make the operation atomic.

`calendarEvent.attendees` is the formatted list returned from `formatCalEvent(calEvent)`, but `newGuests` is the raw caller-supplied array. If `formatCalEvent` normalizes email casing (or trims/strips display-name suffixes), `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` will silently mis-classify a new guest as an existing attendee (or vice-versa), causing the wrong email template to be sent. Both sides of the comparison must go through the same normalization.

Email To header uses empty name for newly-added guests and can crash senders

`to: `${this.attendee.name} <${this.attendee.email}>`` is built unconditionally. The handler inserts new attendees with `name: ""` (`addGuests.handler.ts:85`), so every new-guest email is addressed as ` <new@example.com>`, which most SMTP servers reject as malformed. New guests should have a name populated (or the formatter should fall back to the local part of the email).

Subject reads attendees[0].name without guarding empty array

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` if `attendees` is empty (e.g. an organizer-only booking or a booking whose attendees were wiped before this code path runs). It also produces a blank name in the subject for any new-guest-led booking where the first attendee was inserted with `name: ""`.

Inline Zod schema diverges from the backend schema and validates case-sensitively

The dialog defines its own `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(... set uniqueness ...)` which is case-sensitive (`Set('A@x')` and `Set('a@x')` are different keys) and duplicates the rules from `addGuests.schema.ts`. If the two schemas drift, the user sees a confusing 'Emails must be unique and valid' error even when only one specific field is empty/invalid, and the backend may accept what the frontend rejected. The schema should live in a shared module and lower-case emails before the uniqueness check.

User-facing error toast prefixes the tRPC error code and raw translation key

`showToast(`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, 'error')` exposes internal codes like `BAD_REQUEST: booking_not_found` (because `booking_not_found` is not present in the locale file, so `t()` returns the raw key) directly to end users. The fallback `t("unable_to_add_guests")` is only reached when the constructed string is falsy, which it never is. The toast should display the translated message and use the generic fallback when translation is missing.

Returns a hard-coded English success message instead of the i18n key

The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`. Other handlers in this router return translation keys (e.g. `booking_confirmation_success`) that the client renders via `t()`. Returning an English string here breaks localization and the toast on success (`t("guests_added")`) is wired separately, so the API contract is inconsistent with the rest of the bookings router.

No tests added for a new mutating handler that touches DB, calendar and email

The handler introduces an end-to-end flow with multiple non-trivial branches: permission check (organizer / attendee / team admin / team owner, including the && vs || bug above), blacklist filtering, duplicate attendee detection across casing, calendar sync ordering, and email dispatch for organizer / team members / new guests / existing attendees. None of these paths are exercised by tests in this PR. Given the security-sensitive nature of the changes (any authed user can mutate a booking's attendee list), at least the permission branches, status guard (once added), and the `sendAddGuestsEmails` recipient classification must be covered.

They do not cover: (1) the legitimate-translation case where English has HTML and target has the same HTML (which should pass); (2) case-insensitive HTML in the English source; (3) HTML-like placeholders such as `<NAME>` or `<USERNAME>` in messages that are not whitelisted in `normalizeValue`; (4) multiple anchors; (5) anchors that differ only in inner text but keep the same URL (legitimate translations of link text); (6) `errorTitleHtml`-style keys where the English contains `<strong>` and the translation must keep it. Adding these tests would catch regressions in the sanitizer logic and the normalization rules.

normalizeValue special-cases only a few keys, risking false positives

`normalizeValue` strips HTML-looking content only for `templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit*`, and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`. Any other message that legitimately contains text resembling an HTML tag (e.g., `<NAME>`, `<USERNAME>`, `<EMAIL>`, or any other MessageFormat placeholder that the translator chose to write with angle brackets) will be stripped by the OWASP sanitizer under POLICY_NO_HTML and the verifier will incorrectly report `Illegal HTML`. For example, any key like `fooBarTemplate=Hello <NAME>` will fail verification because `<NAME>` is not an allowed tag. Either broaden the placeholder normalization or detect via the sanitizer whether the English contains any disallowed HTML before applying POLICY_NO_HTML (i.e., compare normalized values against sanitized English, not against the raw translation).

In the new isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut) matcher: (a) the condition is inverted ('return false' when the substring equals the expected grant), and (b) the offset is wrong. The token id format produced by encodeTokenId is ST(2) + TT(2) + GT(2) + ':' + rawId, so the grant shortcut occupies characters at 0-indexed positions 4 and 5 (substring(4,6)). The matcher uses substring(3,5), which is the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant type ("ta" for the example in the PR description, "ac" would actually be at substring(4,6)). Because of the offset, the substring will never equal the expected grant, and because of the inversion the branch returns false instead of true even if it did. As a result, every call site that now uses isAccessTokenId(...) (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) effectively only checks that the token id has the form 'XXXXXX:UUID' and does not actually verify the grant type. The whole point of these test changes - to detect wrong grant shortcut mapping after this PR - is silently lost.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract method on the grant SPI breaks every external implementation

Adding String getShortcut() as an abstract method on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a binary- and source-incompatible change for every third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation (including in the many extensions Keycloak ships). Any out-of-tree impl compiled against the previous version will fail to load at runtime with AbstractMethodError and any extension maintainer will fail to compile against the new version. The field is internal SPI (server-spi-private), but it is still on an interface implemented by SPIs in extension points (Ciba, Device, TokenExchange, UMA Permission, etc.). At a minimum the new method needs a default implementation (e.g. default returning getId()) and the existing built-in factories should override it.

Removed public Context copy constructor

The diff removes the public Context(Context context) copy constructor from OAuth2GrantType.Context (the rest of the constructors remain). Even for 'internal' SPI in the server-spi-private module, this is a binary-incompatible removal: existing compiled callsites and any extension using that constructor will fail with NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If a copy constructor was no longer needed, that should be confirmed; if it was, it should be retained.

getShouldUseLightweightToken promoted from package-private instance to public static

The method signature was changed from 'boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(KeycloakSession session)' (package-private instance) to 'public static boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(KeycloakSession session)'. Subclasses outside this package that overrode the package-private instance version will now have two distinct methods (the inherited one and their override) and call sites using their subclass reference would still hit the parent's version. It would be safer to keep an instance-method shim (e.g. protected boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(...) that delegates to a public static) so that subclasses continue to work, or document and version the change explicitly.

In postInit the loop does grantsByShortcuts.put(grantShortcut, grantName) for each grant. If two factories return the same shortcut, the later entry silently overwrites the earlier one in grantsByShortcuts, but grantsToShortcuts still contains both grant ids. The only validation is the post-loop size check, which catches it but the exception message just says 'Make sure there is no OAuth2GrantType implementation with same ID or shortcut like other grants' and does not identify which shortcut collided. The same race exists in getShortcutByGrantType (lazy refresh path), which does grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType) and grantsToShortcuts.put(grantType, shortcut) without any uniqueness check on the shortcut. If a misbehaving third-party provider returns a shortcut that collides with an existing one, this will silently corrupt the cached mapping at runtime.

Constants.GRANT_TYPE is only set on the refresh path, not consistently on all token-issuance paths

The grant-type attribute is set in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType.process, StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient, PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process, and (for refresh) TokenManager.validateToken. Any future caller of TokenManager.createClientAccessToken / initToken that does not first call one of these will silently fall back to the 'na' (unknown) shortcut in the encoded JTI. Constants.GRANT_TYPE is documented as the canonical key, but the responsibility for populating it is spread across many call sites with no guard. This should either be enforced inside createClientAccessToken/initToken (refuse to issue without a known grant type) or documented; otherwise the encoding will appear to work yet the encoded grant type will be 'na' for missed paths.

getTokenContextFromTokenId(encodedTokenId) calls encodedTokenId.indexOf(':') without a null check. If it is called with a null token id (e.g. a token whose jti claim ended up null/unset, which is possible when no raw id was supplied), it will throw NullPointerException instead of returning the UNKNOWN context. Also, the decoder accepts 'no colon' strings of any length (including empty string) and treats the whole input as the raw id, which means a malformed token id that contains a colon later in the string (rather than as separator) could be parsed incorrectly because indexOf only finds the first ':'.

The new grantType field is initialized once in the constructor from formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE), but the class still exposes setFormParams(...) which replaces the entire formParams map without updating grantType. Any flow that calls setFormParams after construction (the existence of that setter suggests it happens) will leave grantType pointing at the original form value, while getFormParams() returns the new one. The downstream constant Constants.GRANT_TYPE will then be the stale value, and the encoded JTI will carry the wrong grant shortcut.

If `readLength()` returns -1 (the indefinite-length form per X.690), the loop condition `while (length > 0)` is never entered (since -1 > 0 is false) and an empty `List` is returned without raising an error. DER forbids indefinite-length encoding, so encountering it indicates a malformed or non-DER input — silently returning an empty list masks the bug and lets the caller continue processing a bogus signature. The method should throw IOException when `length == -1`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify incorrect handling of the -1 length returned for indefinite-length encoding, resulting in improper processing of encoded data. The candidate describes the skipped loop and empty result rather than the golden comment's subtraction concern, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Breaking API change: order() added as abstract method

The new int order() method is added to the CryptoProvider interface as an abstract method with no default implementation. Any third-party implementation of CryptoProvider will fail to compile against this SPI. A default (e.g., `default int order() { return 100; }`) would preserve existing implementations while letting the in-tree providers (Default/FIPS/Elytron at 200, AuthzClient at 100) override it as needed. As-is, every external CryptoProvider consumer must be updated simultaneously.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding order() as an abstract method to CryptoProvider forces existing implementations to implement it, potentially breaking compilation.

Add an assertion that re-assembles a Signature from the converted bytes and runs `signature.verify()` against the original data and public key; also test negative cases (tampered DER, wrong length).

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is not joined before asserting caughtExceptions

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti, the reader thread is started with `new Thread(() -> {...}).start()` without storing the reference, and the main thread sets `deletedAll.set(true)` and then immediately asserts `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())`. If the reader thread is still executing a `groups(...)` call when the assertion runs, any exception it subsequently catches is written to caughtExceptions after the assertion has already been evaluated, causing the test to silently miss failures. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the main thread sets deletedAll and asserts caughtExceptions without waiting for the reader thread, allowing later exceptions to be missed and making the test flaky.

false_positives.candidate:
_create_process_for_shard is dead code

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined but never called anywhere in the codebase. Restarts are done via `_ensure_processes_alive`, which calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This leftover method just adds noise and may mislead future maintainers into thinking shard-level restart is wired up when it is not.

Docstring claims 'one process per shard' but CLI default yields 1 process total

The class docstring reads: 'A background multiprocessing manager that polls Redis for new segments to flush and to produce to Kafka. Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' However, the CLI option registered for `process-spans` defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, and the factory forwards that value unchanged. With the production default, self.max_processes == 1, so all assigned shards end up on a single process (process_to_shards_map[0] holds every shard). The docstring is therefore misleading for any deployment that does not explicitly raise `--flusher-processes` to at least len(assigned_shards). Either update the docstring to describe the actual default ('up to N processes; default N=1 means one process handles all shards') or change the CLI default to None so the per-shard behavior is enabled out of the box.

CLI help for --flusher-processes contradicts PR goal

The new click option is documented as: 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' The PR description says the goal is to 'spawn a process per redis shard'. A reader who wants per-shard processing has no hint from this help text that they must set `--flusher-processes` to a value >= the number of shards; otherwise every shard shares one process. Either rewrite the help to make the relationship to shard count explicit, or change the default so that the stated goal is achieved without operator action.

test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts configuration, not behaviour

The new test creates the factory with flusher_processes=2 and 4 partitions, then asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that the total shards across the process_to_shards_map equals 4. It never submits any Kafka message, never advances `current_drift`, never verifies that any of the two flusher threads actually flush a segment, and never asserts how the shards are split between the two processes (e.g., process 0 -> [0,2], process 1 -> [1,3]). It also does not cover the edge cases the new code introduces: flusher_processes=None, flusher_processes=0, flusher_processes >= number of shards, or an explicit per-shard assignment. Without functional coverage the multi-process path could silently regress (e.g., shards never being flushed because the buffer-per-shard mapping is wrong) without any test failing.

`if not process:` guard is dead code

Inside `_ensure_processes_alive`, the loop has `if not process: continue`, but the dict `self.processes` is only ever assigned via `_create_process_for_shards`, which stores the object returned by `make_process(...)` (either `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` or `threading.Thread`). Both are always truthy after their constructor returns, so the guard is never taken. It can be removed to avoid implying that None/False values may appear here.

num_processes=0 with no shards silently disables the flusher

`self.num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` evaluates to 0 when the buffer has zero assigned shards. `_create_processes()` then iterates over an empty mapping, so `self.processes`, `self.process_healthy_since`, `self.process_backpressure_since`, `process_restarts`, and `self.buffers` all stay empty. Later in `submit()` the loops over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` and `self.buffers.values()` are also empty, so no backpressure is ever reported, no `record_stored_segments` metric is emitted, and no process liveness is enforced. If the consumer can ever be constructed with zero partitions (e.g., during a brief rebalance window or misconfiguration), the flusher silently becomes a no-op and segments can pile up in Redis with no operator-visible signal. Adding an explicit guard (e.g., skip creating the SpanFlusher, or raise) would surface this state.

This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes same-key builds; risk of corrupted file index

The diff removes the outer `b.cacheMu.Lock(); defer b.cacheMu.Unlock()` that wrapped all of `BuildIndex` and replaces it with a narrow lock around only the `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment. `getOrCreateIndex` calls `s.search.GetIndex` and then `s.build`, so the cache read and the cache update are not atomic. The OLD code at least serialized any two concurrent `BuildIndex` calls for the same key via the global write lock; the NEW code allows them to run in parallel. For file-based indices this is dangerous: `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` opens the same on-disk directory (`filepath.Join(b.opts.Root, key.Namespace, fmt.Sprintf("%s.%s", key.Resource, key.Group))`) in two goroutines, and bleve (bolt/badger-backed) does not safely tolerate concurrent openers/writers on the same path, so the on-disk index can be corrupted and subsequent reads will fail or return garbage. For memory-backed indices, both goroutines still build a full index and the loser is orphaned (CPU + memory leak). The intended concurrency win is for different keys; same-key concurrency needs per-key serialization (e.g. a `sync.Map` of per-key mutexes) before opening the bleve index.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: narrowing b.cacheMu protection to the final cache assignment allows concurrent BuildIndex calls to build the same expensive index for the same key. Its additional claims about file corruption do not change the underlying issue identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads cache without holding the cache lock

`TotalDocs` does `for _, v := range b.cache { ... }` with no lock acquisition, while `BuildIndex` (now able to run concurrently with other builds and with any caller of `TotalDocs`) writes to `b.cache` under `b.cacheMu`. Iterating a Go map while it is being written to is a data race and is documented as able to panic with "fatal error: concurrent map read and map write" or "concurrent map writes". `TotalDocs` is part of the `SearchBackend` interface and is called from `searchSupport.init` via `s.search.TotalDocs()` immediately after `group.Wait()`, but it may also be invoked from elsewhere (metrics endpoints, future callers). It should at least take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` for the duration of the iteration. Previously this was masked because the lock was held during the whole `BuildIndex`; with the finer-grained locking the race window is now larger.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while concurrent BuildIndex calls may write to it, creating a data race and potential concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate also identifies the same TotalDocs call in searchSupport.init.

false_positives.candidate:
Init triggers two WatchWriteEvents calls; SQL backend spawns two pollers

`(*server).Init` is now called from `NewResourceServer` and unconditionally runs both `s.search.init(ctx)` and `s.initWatcher()`. `search.init` itself calls `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)` and starts a long-lived goroutine that consumes from that channel. `initWatcher` then constructs a `Broadcaster` whose subscriber-setup callback also calls `s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)` the first time a client subscribes via `Watch`. For the SQL backend, `WatchWriteEvents` is implemented as `go b.poller(ctx, since, stream)` (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:566), so every call spins up a new poller goroutine that polls the database every 100ms. After this PR, every Grafana process with unified storage enabled runs two such pollers against the same database and reads the same history rows, doubling query load and (for `search.init`'s consumer) processing events from a completely separate stream than the `Broadcaster`. The PR explicitly reorders the init code but does not address this; the right fix is to have `search.init` subscribe to the existing `Broadcaster` instead of opening a second watcher. This was pre-existing but is directly within the scope of the init restructuring and should be resolved in the same change.

NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and leaks partial state on Init failure

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` if it fails. There are three consequences a maintainer should be aware of: (1) every caller of the constructor now blocks for as long as it takes to build every search index, which is a contract change from the previous "return fast, build on first gRPC call" behavior; this can affect test fixtures, alternate startup paths, and any code that constructs a `ResourceServer` and expects immediate return. (2) If `search.init` fails partway through, indexes that were successfully built remain in the bleve cache and any partially-started watcher goroutine is not torn down, because `Stop` is not called when returning `(nil, err)`. false_positives.candidate:
OffsetTracker commits past unseen offsets, causing silent data loss

In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed` (lines 100–105), after committing offset X, all offsets ≤ X are removed from `self.all_offsets`. On the next `get_committable_offsets` call, the loop starts at `max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets))`, so any offset that was never submitted to the tracker is forgotten. If the consumer skips an offset (e.g., 101) but submits 100, 102, 103, the tracker will first commit 100 then, after removal, commit 103 — committing past the unseen 101 to Kafka. On restart, Kafka would begin reading from offset 104, permanently losing offset 101. The tracker assumes gaps are always due to filtering/compaction, but it has no way to distinguish that from a bug where `submit()` was never called for an offset. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py` was clearly designed to catch this behavior (it asserts commits never exceed 101), but the implementation violates that assertion — the last commit would be 104. A safer design would either keep removed offsets to detect gaps, or require every offset in [last_committed, X] to have been at least seen.

The file uses `queue.ShutDown` (caught in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` lines 132 and 142) and `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (line 238). Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were introduced in Python 3.13 (October 2024). If sentry still supports Python 3.11 or 3.12, the workers will crash with `AttributeError: module 'queue' has no attribute 'ShutDown'` / `'shutdown'` the first time a shutdown is attempted or an exception is raised inside `run()`. The minimum Python version supported by sentry needs to be verified; if it is below 3.13, this module cannot be imported safely and will break the uptime-results consumer at runtime. A portable alternative is to use a sentinel object via `Queue.put` and check it in the worker, or a `threading.Event` plus a final empty marker, neither requiring Python 3.13.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate does not join commit thread

`terminate` sets `shutdown_event` and calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but unlike `close` it never calls `self.commit_thread.join(...)`. The commit thread is daemonized, so the process exit will reap it, but during the window between `terminate` returning and the process actually exiting, the commit thread can still invoke `self.commit_function` (the arroyo `commit` callback) and mutate `OffsetTracker` state. This violates the symmetry with `close`, and means callers using `terminate` for a forced shutdown can have an arbitrary amount of background work still running against a strategy they consider terminated.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout argument

`join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` simply calls `self.close()`, dropping the `timeout` parameter. `close()` in turn calls `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` (hard-coded 5s) and `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (which joins workers with another hard-coded 5s). Callers that pass a smaller timeout via `join(0.5)` expecting bounded shutdown will wait up to ~10 seconds instead. The `timeout` argument should either be honored by passing it to the underlying joins or removed from the signature.

test_different_groups_distributed is probabilistic and can be flaky

The test submits 20 distinct group keys to a pool of 3 queues and asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3`. The probability of missing a queue with 20 keys and 3 buckets is 3 * (2/3)^20 - 3 * (1/3)^20 ≈ 0.00078, or about 1 in 1300. With Python's randomized string hashing (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) this is not controllable from the test. Worse, `hash()` can in principle produce collisions that bunch keys into fewer buckets than expected. The test should either use enough keys that the probability of collision is negligible (e.g. 200+), or directly assert `>= 2` rather than `== 3`, or seed/force the hash distribution.

Kafka integration test relies on private methods and tight timing

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` reaches into `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private Arroyo APIs) and only spins for 5 seconds before asserting `committed[0].offset == 5`. Under load or slow CI the consumer may not have time to fetch, decode, queue, and commit all 5 messages; the assertion then fails for timing reasons rather than correctness. Additionally, the test wraps `factory.create_with_partitions` to count commits but does not verify that all produced messages were actually decoded (`mock_processor.return_value = None` bypasses real processing). Consider using Arroyo's public `run()` loop, increasing the deadline, and asserting a lower bound (e.g. offset >= 1) rather than equality.

The new code uses `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with subscript access, while every other optional field in the same Span constructor (parent_span_id, is_remote) uses `.get()`. Any span payload already buffered in the ingest-spans Kafka topic (or coming from a producer that has not yet been upgraded) that lacks this key will raise KeyError and crash the consumer batch. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` (or fall back to a sentinel such as 0.0) for forward compatibility with in-flight messages.

max_segment_spans protection silently removed from flush path

`_load_segment_data` previously guarded against runaway segments by deleting any key whose accumulated span count exceeded `self.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and emitting the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric. The diff deletes that branch entirely and the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is now dead — no code reads it. The new in-Lua `zpopmin` eviction runs on the insert path, but it does not protect against (a) segments populated before this rollout, (b) sets that exceed 1000 entries between two insert calls, or (c) the case where `zcard(set_key)` after `zunionstore` returns 0 because both source sets were empty (so eviction is skipped even though `zcard` afterward would still report >1000). Without the flush-time guard a single oversized segment will now be loaded into memory and serialized, which is exactly what the old check prevented.

zpopmin eviction key is not actually oldest spans

Eviction uses `zpopmin` against `end_timestamp_precise` scores. When many spans in a segment share the same `end_timestamp_precise` (which is the common case for spans belonging to the same transaction), Redis sorted-set ordering for ties is lexicographic on the member bytes, i.e. on the JSON payload. The "evict oldest" policy therefore degenerates to "evict whichever serialized payload sorts first," which is essentially arbitrary and may preferentially drop small/different payloads. The score should include a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g. span_id) so eviction order is reproducible.

OptimizedCursorPaginator added with no test coverage

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result with a security-relevant behavior change (allowing negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features=True`). It is wired into the audit-logs endpoint and gated only by `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but there are zero tests for the class itself, for `enable_advanced_features=True` path, for negative offsets, or for the auditlog endpoint's new `optimized_pagination=true` branch. A paginator that silently changes the cursor contract for admins deserves its own tests in tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py and tests/sentry/api/endpoints/test_organization_auditlogs.py.

In `BasePaginator.build_queryset` the branch that flips `-key` ordering back to ascending writes `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — `order_b` is not an attribute of `Query` (the correct attribute is `order_by`). As a result, the reversed ordering is silently dropped and the queryset is left ordered by `-key` even though the code intended `+key`. This is in the same file the diff touches and is exercised by every caller using a descending order_by with a `is_prev=True` cursor that has a cursor value. It must be fixed before this PR lands; the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` inherits from `BasePaginator` and inherits the bug.

The endpoint change is labeled "Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns" and the new query parameter is named `optimized_pagination`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator` produces the same SQL plan as `DateTimePaginator` for the normal (forward, non-negative offset) case; the only functional difference is that it permits negative cursor offsets. There is no benchmark, no documentation in `api-docs/` (Sentry typically gates new query params), and no mention that the new branch is only active for superusers/org members with global access — `enable_advanced_features=True` is silently enabled based on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, which is not the same permission check used elsewhere in this endpoint (`OrganizationAuditPermission`). upsampled_count SnQLFunction not marked private

The newly added `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, unlike the surrounding private helpers (e.g. `thing_expression`, `count_at_least`). Without that flag the function becomes part of the user-exposed SnQL/Discover function surface, so end users could write `upsampled_count()` in their own queries. The function is only meaningful in conjunction with the project allowlist/sampling-rate pipeline, and emits `sum(sample_weight)` which has different semantics (and potential NULL-handling) from `count()`. Users invoking it directly outside of `organization_events_stats` will get counts that silently diverge from what they expect.

sum(sample_weight) silently drops NULL sample_weight rows

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count()` which is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse/SnQL `sum` ignores NULL arguments entirely, so any allowlisted-project event that has `sample_weight IS NULL` is silently omitted from the result, undercounting errors. The comment claims the schema guarantees `sample_weight` is non-null for allowlisted projects, but nothing in this helper (or in `discover.py`) enforces or even validates that invariant. There should be at minimum a guard that rejects the transformation (or coalesces `sample_weight` to a fallback) when the project list could contain NULL-weight events, otherwise dashboards/alerts that switch to upsampled counts will report numbers lower than the truth with no warning.

transform only matches literal count(), misses aliased and surrounded variants

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` compares `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. This single-equality test misses common variants that should still be upsampled: `count() as my_count`, `count() AS errors`, `count("id")` (counting a specific column), or `count()` surrounded by extra inner whitespace. As a result, a column written as `count() as count` (with explicit alias) will be passed through unchanged while the same column written as `count()` will be replaced with `upsampled_count() as count`, giving two clients querying the same metric different aggregations. The transform should at least recognise `count()` with a trailing `as <alias>` clause.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring match on query string

`_is_error_focused_query` decides based on `"event.type:error" in query`. The check is a raw substring match, so queries like `event.type:error_handled` (if such an alias is ever introduced) or any token that begins with `event.type:error` would be treated as error-focused and force the upsampled transformation on a dataset that may include non-error rows. A safer check parses the query tokens (e.g. via `event_search.parse_search_query`) and inspects the actual `event.type` value rather than doing a substring `in`.

Error message wording regression adjacent to top_events validation

The diff changes the response message from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. The new wording is grammatically cleaner, but it is bundled into a commit titled `feat(upsampling)` with no mention of an API/UX message change. Because this is a public 400 response body on `organization-events-stats`, any client that does an exact-string match on this `detail` value (e.g. localised tooling) will break. The change should either be split into its own commit or called out in the description.

Unnecessary try/except around safe dict lookups

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps the chained `.get(...).get(...).get(...)` in a `try/except Exception: pass` and the `float(...)` conversion in another one. `dict.get` cannot raise for missing keys, and a malformed `client_sample_rate` string is the only realistic failure mode, which the second `try` already handles. The first try/except hides real bugs (e.g. `AttributeError` from a malformed contexts payload) and should be removed; only the `float()` conversion needs to be defensive.

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, the test calls `self.login_as(user=self.user)` with the user that `APITestCase.setUp` created, then immediately overwrites `self.user = self.create_user()`. From that point on, `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user, and any tag, audit log entry, or future test that reads `self.user` will silently use the wrong identity. In particular the events stored right below use `self.user.email` / `self.user2.email` as the `sentry:user` tag, which means the test is asserting counts against events whose owner does not match the calling API user; if any later assertion (or downstream test) compares user identity this will fail.

Stale upsampling eligibility cache has no invalidation hook

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the all-projects-in-allowlist result for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is provided but never called from anywhere in the diff (no admin signal, option listener, or tests cover invalidation). If a project is added to or removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, requests for the next minute will continue to use the previous decision. In the worst case (allowlist shrinks while cache still says eligible) the endpoint will issue `sum(sample_weight)` queries for projects that no longer guarantee non-null `sample_weight`, potentially producing the silent undercount called out above. There should be an explicit invalidation call (or a much shorter TTL, or no cache) wired up before merging.

Tests do not cover caching, invalidation, aliased count(), or NULL sample_weight

The new test file covers the allowlist membership, the basic `count()` transform, the `event.type:error` substring check, and the dataset dispatch, but misses the most failure-prone paths: (1) `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is never tested, so the cache key construction (`hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`), cache-hit fast path, and 60s TTL behaviour are entirely uncovered; (2) `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` is never given aliased inputs (`count() as my_count`) so the limitation called out above is not pinned by a test; (3) there is no test asserting behaviour when a project in the allowlist emits events without `sample_weight`. Adding at least one cache-hit/miss test and an aliased-count test would prevent the cache and transform edge cases from regressing unnoticed.

The cache key is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. While `hash(int)` is deterministic in CPython, mixing `hash()` of a derived structure into a cache key is fragile (it depends on tuple-hash internals and any future changes to them) and produces opaque keys that are hard to inspect/grep in Redis. A deterministic, explicit key like `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))}"` (or a sha1 prefix) would be safer, debuggable, and immune to future interpreter changes.

The current naming userPermDenialCacheKey also misleads readers into thinking it only applies to real users.

Permission-denial cache can mask newly granted access for up to 30s

In Service.Check, when the DB lookup returns !allowed, the (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) tuple is written to permDenialCache with shortCacheTTL (30s). On any subsequent request for that exact tuple within the TTL, the denial cache short-circuits and returns Allowed=false without consulting permCache or the DB. This means workflows where a user gains access to a previously denied resource (e.g., an admin assigning a role that grants dashboards:read on a specific dashboard, or a service account being granted a folder) will be incorrectly denied for up to 30 seconds after the grant, despite the PR's stated goal of letting newly created dashboards/folders be accessible. Either the TTL needs to be much shorter, the denial cache must not be consulted before the permCache/DB for the freshly granted case, or some form of invalidation is required when permissions change.

The new permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", action).Inc() call in Service.Check is reached both on a permCache miss (err != nil from getCachedIdentityPermissions) AND on a permCache hit that denies the request. In both cases we fall through to a getIdentityPermissions DB query. So the metric really tracks "did we have to query the DB", not "was the cache hit/missed". Combined with the symmetric requestCount.WithLabelValues(..., "true", ...) which is incremented on every code path after validateCheckRequest succeeds (cache hits, cache misses that went to DB, and errors during/after the DB call), the label "cached" is misleading. Either rename the labels (e.g., "served_from_db") or restrict "true" to genuine cache-hit responses so dashboards and alerts derived from these counters are meaningful.

Existing "should deny user without permission" test does not verify the new denial cache population

TestService_Check "User permission check" / "Anonymous permission check" already exercises the path that should populate permDenialCache (a Check that returns Allowed=false after going through getIdentityPermissions), but the assertions only check idCache and permCache, never permDenialCache. With the new code, a successful denial on the slow path must result in an entry under userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, userUID, action, name, parent); the test should assert that presence so that any future regression that drops the Set call is caught.

"Fallback to the database on outdated cache" test does not verify the cache was refreshed

The sub-test pre-seeds permCache with an outdated entry for dashboards:read (only dash1) and a DB that grants dash2, expecting Allowed=true via the fallback path. It does not assert that permCache was updated with the freshly fetched scopes including "dashboards:uid:dash2". Since the whole point of the fallback path is to keep permCache fresh, this should be asserted (e.g. require.Contains on s.permCache.Get for the new key).

NoopCache methods have unused ctx parameter and unused receiver name

The new NoopCache.Get/Set/Delete all declare ctx context.Context but never reference it, and the receiver is named lc (a leftover from LocalCache). Pass-though no-op types typically either omit the parameter (using the cache.Cache contract that doesn't require it) or use _ = ctx; the current shape will trigger unused-parameter linters and obscures the intent that these are pure no-ops. A short doc comment on the type explaining why this exists (in-proc client wants to skip the authlib local cache because the in-process server is already caching) would also help reviewers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

Users filing a request to "implement SQL expressions" or assuming it will arrive in a future release is a foreseeable miscommunication. Consider wording such as "sqlExpressions are disabled for security reasons (see CVE-2024-9264)" or, at minimum, "sqlExpressions are not supported in this version" so users understand this is an intentional, security-driven removal and not a missing feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes redundant recomputation under concurrent first-time load

After taking the write lock at line 48, the function does not re-check whether another goroutine has populated `entryPointAssetsCache` while this goroutine was waiting for the lock. In non-Dev mode with an initially empty cache, multiple concurrent first-time callers will all see `nil` under the read lock, enter the write path, serialize on the write lock, and each independently re-read and re-parse the manifest and overwrite the cache. The consequence is wasted I/O and CPU at startup. Add a second check under the write lock so only the first caller does the work:

entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()
defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()
if entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev {
    return entryPointAssetsCache, nil
}

Additionally, the write path unconditionally overwrites the cache with `result` even when `readWebAssetsFromFile` returns an error (result == nil, err != nil). This pre-existing cache-poisoning bug is now reachable from concurrent requests: one goroutine's transient failure can evict a previously valid cache value, forcing every subsequent caller to retry the file read. The error path should leave the previous cache value intact.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: failing to re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate it. The additional error-path concern does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute, unrelated to deadlock fix

The ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1 with no comment and no relation to the MySQL deadlock being addressed. This is a 10x increase in how often the cleanup job runs, and combined with this PR's split-into-two-statements change each cleanup now performs roughly 2x more DB round trips per batch. On large annotation tables this can substantially increase database load, lock contention, and log volume. The 9-minute cleanup context timeout also means a single slow run (made slower by the new strategy) is much more likely to be cancelled. This belongs in its own PR with justification, or at least a comment explaining the rationale, and ideally should be configurable rather than a hard-coded 1-minute default.

false_positives.candidate:
annotationType interpolated into SQL without validation

In CleanAnnotations, the annotationType argument is interpolated directly into the WHERE clause via fmt.Sprintf: cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, ...). annotationType is an interface-typed string parameter with no allow-list or validation in fetchIDs; any caller passing untrusted input gets a SQL injection. This pattern was inherited from the old code but is now reused via fetchIDs which itself does fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition). At minimum the helpers should reject table/condition values that don't match an expected allow-list or constant set (e.g. alertAnnotationType, dashboardAnnotationType, apiAnnotationType), or the SQL should be composed with bound parameters instead of string formatting.

O(n^2) string building in SQLite inline-id path

In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size > 999, the code builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf('%s, %d', values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration allocates a new string of length O(i), giving O(n^2) work and O(n^2) intermediate allocations. For a batch of 32767 IDs this is on the order of a billion character copies. Use strings.Builder or a single fmt.Sprintf with a precomputed separator, or strings.Join over strconv formatted values. The new integration test exercises exactly this path with 32767 IDs, so the cost will show up in CI and any production SQLite deployment configured with a large batch size.

deleteByIDs chooses inlined SQL by configured batch size, not actual id count

deleteByIDs switches to the inlined-SQL branch when r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit. The branch should depend on len(ids), not on the configured batch size: if the operator has set a large batch size but a particular batch returns only a handful of ids (common when there are few rows left to clean), we still go down the inlined-SQL path and pay the O(n^2) cost for no benefit. Conversely, if the operator mis-configures AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to be small (<= 999) while the actual returned ids somehow exceed that (e.g. via a future change), we would silently use the parameterized path and potentially exceed SQLite's parameter limit. Use len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit as the gate.

After fetching the ids, the delete runs in a separate statement and separate session. A concurrent transaction can insert new annotations that satisfy the same cleanup predicate (MaxAge cutoff or MaxCount offset) between fetch and delete; those new rows will not be in the fetched id set and so will not be deleted this cycle. The author documented this as 'may under-delete... any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle', which is acceptable, but the test suite does not exercise this scenario (no concurrent inserter) and there is no log/instrumentation that would let an operator detect persistent under-deletion. Worth noting so it isn't quietly relied on as exact enforcement.

t.Cleanup uses assert.NoError, failures don't terminate subsequent subtests

The new per-subtest t.Cleanup deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows via session.Exec and then calls assert.NoError(t, err). assert.NoError only records t.Error and does not call t.FailNow, so if the DELETE silently fails (e.g., a SQL error in a future schema change), the next subtest will run against leftover data and produce confusing failures rather than failing at the cleanup site. Use require.NoError inside the cleanup so a failure surfaces immediately. Also, the subtests share the same fakeSQL but rely on sequential DELETE before the next subtest creates ids starting from 1; a missed cleanup causes primary-key conflicts on subsequent InsertMulti.

New SQLite large-batch test is slow and may run unconditionally

The new subtest 'should not fail if batch size is larger than SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER for SQLite >= 3.32.0' creates 40003 annotations and 80006 annotation_tags, then performs a multi-batch cleanup. createTestAnnotations uses InsertMulti in batches of 500, so this requires ~80 annotation batches and ~161 tag batches, plus several cleanup cycles. This is fine on developer laptops but will add noticeable seconds to every CI run on this package. There is no t.Skip on this case and the assertion (40000 affected) depends on the exact i%3 split working out, which is fragile if the createTestAnnotations layout changes. Consider a smaller number or guarding it behind a build tag.

The previously-in-package TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst were renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp and TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst and gained a t.Skip on testing.Short(). The earlier versions ran unconditionally and provided coverage of the cleanup SQL; the new versions are gated on a long mode and require the InitTestDB infra. There is no replacement test that covers the SQL composition (the cond strings, the annotationType interpolation, the MaxCount offset arithmetic) without a DB, and no test that specifically asserts the deadlock-avoidance split (id fetch + separate delete) is exercised. At minimum a table-driven unit test verifying the constructed cond strings and the Limit/LimitOffset substitution for each dialect would prevent silent regressions to the SQL the PR is trying to fix.

The split sub-requests are then dispatched with the full-range literal inside the expression but a per-chunk time range, so each sub-query computes its rate over the wrong window and the merged result is incorrect. Before this PR the original `$__range` token was still present when `querySupportsSplitting` ran, so the exclusion worked; this PR silently bypasses it.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race lets device count exceed the configured limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then either updateDevice or an INSERT as two separate, non-atomic steps (lines 109-118 and the switch/INSERT at 120-153). Under concurrent anonymous authentications many goroutines can each observe count < deviceLimit, all proceed to insert, and the resulting count can exceed deviceLimit by the concurrency level. This defeats the stated purpose of the feature — the limit is not a hard cap but only an approximate one, and a burst of legitimate users (or a small attacker) can inflate the table well past it. Wrap the check and write in a single transaction (or use a serializable isolation level / advisory lock) so the limit is enforced atomically.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the configured limit. Both recommend a transaction or lock to enforce the limit atomically.

true_positives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice uses device.UpdatedAt as its time reference while CreateOrUpdateDevice uses time.Now()

In CreateOrUpdateDevice the 30-day window is built from time.Now().UTC() (line 110), but in updateDevice the WHERE bounds on updated_at are built from device.UpdatedAt.UTC() (lines 80-81). They happen to coincide today because TagDevice constructs the Device with UpdatedAt: time.Now() (impl.go line 141), but the two functions now disagree on what 'now' is. If a future caller passes a Device whose UpdatedAt is anything other than time.Now() (a replay, a clock-skew tolerance, a test fixture, a backfill, or simply a refactor), the updateDevice bounds will silently drift relative to the count window: a device that should be considered 'recent' by CreateOrUpdateDevice can be excluded by updateDevice and vice versa. Capture time.Now() once at the start of CreateOrUpdateDevice and pass it (or device.UpdatedAt derived from it) into updateDevice explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify inconsistent time references in the expiration window involving device.UpdatedAt and recommend using a consistent time.Now().UTC()-based reference. The candidate expands on the potential consequences of that same inconsistency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit bypassed on retry via local cache

In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set on line 87 with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) BEFORE the CreateOrUpdateDevice DB call. When the device limit is reached and that DB call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry is already populated. Any subsequent request from the same client within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the cache (line 83), returns nil immediately, and Authenticate proceeds — bypassing the limit entirely. The limit is therefore only enforced on the very first request for a given device ID; a single retry lets the user through. To actually enforce it, the cache must only be populated after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (or the cache key must encode the limit-reached state). This regression is introduced by the new ErrDeviceLimitReached path: the cache pattern was harmless before because all errors were swallowed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the cache populated after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing retries to bypass the device limit during the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now blocks synchronously on TagDevice DB writes

Previously TagDevice was called in a goroutine with a 2-minute context timeout, so Anonymous.Authenticate returned after one DB lookup (orgService.GetByName). The new code calls TagDevice synchronously at line 44, which internally runs CountDevices (SELECT COUNT(*)) plus an INSERT/UPDATE on anon_device on every anonymous request. Each anonymous authentication now performs 2-3 DB operations instead of 1, and any DB latency or contention is added to auth latency. For Grafana instances that expose anonymous dashboards to high traffic this is a serious performance and reliability regression. The async pattern should be kept; the limit decision can be propagated via a channel, or the CountDevices check alone can be made synchronous while the write stays async.

Device-limit failure surfaces as a bare sentinel error with no HTTP semantics

Anonymous.Authenticate returns the raw sentinel var ErrDeviceLimitReached = fmt.Errorf("device limit reached") (defined in anonstore/database.go line 18) at line 46, with no HTTP status code, no machine-readable code, and no user-facing message. The authn framework will propagate this as a generic authentication failure, almost certainly a 500/Internal-Server-Error-like response to the browser. Operators have no signal that the limit is the cause (they will see only generic auth-failure logs), and end users see no indication that they are hitting a configured cap versus a real outage. Wrap the sentinel in a typed error that carries a 429/503 status and a clear message, or convert it in the HTTP layer so the response makes the cause actionable.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device ID is rejected when the count has reached the limit. The crucial opposite case — a known device ID re-tags while the limit is reached and must be updated successfully via updateDevice — is not tested. This is the only path that uses updateDevice at all in this PR, and a regression that always returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (e.g., the WHERE bounds drifting to exclude every row, as flagged separately) would not be caught. Add a case with deviceLimit=1 that inserts device X, then calls CreateOrUpdateDevice with the same X again (optionally with a slightly different client_ip/user_agent) and asserts no error and that the row was actually updated.

Until those are regenerated the build will fail because the old ProvideAnonDBStore(store) and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService(..., anonStore, ...) calls no longer exist. setting.go adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0) under [auth.anonymous] at line 1650, but no documentation file is changed. The PR description itself leaves the 'docs are updated' checklist item unchecked. Operators have no reference for the new key, its default of 0 (= no limit), or its semantics (when the limit is reached, new anonymous device IDs are rejected while known devices can still re-tag). Add the key to the appropriate configuration reference (e.g. docs/sources/administration/configuration.md) and, if this is a notable improvement, link it from the What's New doc per the PR template.

The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! has a data race on @loaded_locales

ensure_loaded! initializes @loaded_locales ||= [] outside any mutex and then calls load_locale, which itself protects only the body via LOAD_MUTEX. Two threads that race on the first call can each observe @loaded_locales as nil, create separate Array instances, and the last write wins. Whichever instance is no longer referenced loses its additions, so subsequent calls into ensure_loaded!/load_locale can re-load already-loaded locales. The mutex currently held only by load_locale is not sufficient because @loaded_locales may flip between two arrays mid-flight. Initialize the ivar under the same LOAD_MUTEX (or use a Set guarded by the mutex) so the @loaded_locales reference itself is stable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unsynchronized lazy initialization and concurrent access to @loaded_locales in translate_accelerator.rb. The candidate describes the same data race and explains why the mutex in load_locale does not protect initialization.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback chain mixes String and Symbol locales

set_locale in application_controller.rb assigns I18n.locale from current_user.effective_locale or SiteSetting.default_locale, which return String values in Discourse. The fallback chain is [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en], so the chain can contain a String like 'fr' alongside Symbols :en. Array#uniq does not deduplicate values of different types, so 'en' and :en would both end up in the chain and load_locale would add both to @loaded_locales in translate_accelerator.rb. This results in wasted reloads and risks comparison surprises in i18n internals or third-party code. Coerce locale to a Symbol (e.g. locale.to_sym) so the chain is uniformly typed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify inconsistent String versus Symbol locale handling that can cause the same locale to be loaded twice, and recommend normalizing locales to Symbols.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new fallback behavior

The PR introduces a new FallbackLocaleList class, a custom I18n.fallbacks implementation, the new I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! method, and a new I18n.ensure_loaded! method on the freedom patch. None of these changes have accompanying specs. There is no coverage verifying: that the fallback chain order is correct for users vs anonymous requests, that I18n.locale changes between requests trigger reloads, that SiteSetting.default_locale is honored as a fallback, that missing keys in a non-English locale correctly fall back to English, or that ensure_loaded! is idempotent. The PR description 'Test 9' does not indicate tests are present anywhere.

FallbackLocaleList < Hash redefines only the [] method. All other methods of I18n::Locale::Fallbacks that callers may rely on (e.g. defaults, defaults=, compute, map, each over configured fallbacks, []=) are left as plain Hash methods that operate on an always-empty Hash. Any plugin or piece of code that does I18n.fallbacks[:zh_TW] = [:zh_TW, :zh_CN, :en] will silently be ignored because lookup always goes through the overridden []. Methods like I18n.fallbacks.defaults will raise NoMethodError. Either stop inheriting Hash or implement the full Locale::Fallbacks contract so that per-locale configuration and other API consumers are not broken.

set_locale runs as a before_filter on every request, and the new line invokes I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which calls self[I18n.locale] and allocates a new Array every time, then iterates it calling I18n.ensure_loaded! for each fallback locale.
