They do not cover: (a) the second branch where both hosts have the same number of parts greater than two (e.g. `www.example.com` vs `forum.example.com`) and a non-matching second-level label; (b) websites whose path includes a query string or fragment, to verify whether they are preserved or dropped; (c) websites with a non-default port; (d) websites whose scheme is missing or unparseable, to verify the `rescue nil` path doesn't leak garbage. None of these are covered by the existing TL0/untrusted test either, so the privacy regression on `:website_name` going through without `untrusted_attributes` is also untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring indexOf instead of a real origin comparison

`if (discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1) { return; }` only confirms that e.origin appears as a substring of discourseUrl. Any e.origin that is a substring of whatever `discourseUrl` is configured to (including future paths/queries/cached redirects) will pass the gate and be allowed to set `iframe.height` or drive other future message handlers. Use `new URL(discourseUrl).origin === e.origin` (or compare parsed origins via the postMessage API's own origin field) so the handler accepts only the configured Discourse origin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying security issue: indexOf-based substring validation of postMessage origins can accept an unintended attacker-controlled origin instead of requiring an exact origin match. The candidate describes the substring direction more precisely, but targets the same flawed check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Embed URL injected raw into HTML, enabling XSS in the rendered embed view The embed URL is interpolated unescaped into both the href attribute and the link text via I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}"). Imported posts are persisted with cook_method = :raw_html and the embed view renders their HTML through `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, so the appended markup is emitted verbatim into the discourse origin. An embed URL containing a single quote, a newline, an `on*=` payload, or a `javascript:` scheme (originating from any RSS item, from a CMS at SiteSetting.embeddable_host, or from any direct caller of TopicEmbed.import) breaks out of the `` attribute and runs attacker-supplied HTML/JS. The call also mutates the caller's `contents` string in place via `<<`, which can break frozen-string inputs and corrupts the caller's data. Use Rails' link_to(url) (or html_escape) and build the suffix into a separate String instead of mutating `contents`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by unescaped URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import's generated HTML. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but it directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
<%- end if %> is a SyntaxError in Ruby ERB and will prevent the embed view from rendering

Line 6 closes the first if/else block with `  <%- end if %>`. Inside ERB that compiles to the literal Ruby `end if`, whose `if` modifier requires a condition expression. With no condition following `if`, Ruby's parser raises a SyntaxError the first time the view is compiled, so any request that reaches `best.html.erb` (i.e., any embedded topic that has been imported) will blow up instead of rendering. The other if/else in this same file (lines 11, 22, 29) closes with plain `<%- end %>`, confirming that this is a stray ` if` typo. Replace with `<%- end %>`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the invalid ERB closing statement `end if`, which causes a Ruby syntax error during rendering, and recommend replacing it with plain `end`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
PollFeed job aborts the entire hourly run on the first item or network failure

Inside the `rss.items.each` loop, `i.content.scrub` raises on a nil/Non-String item content, `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` raises on any transient network or HTTP error, and `TopicEmbed.import` raises on URL-regex mismatch or Nokogiri errors from `absolutize_urls`. Combined with `sidekiq_options retry: false`, one malformed item or one bad network response silently drops every subsequent item in the feed until the next hourly cron — and the exceptions are lost because the `feed_polling_enabled?` guard never runs around the loop. Wrap each item (and the open/parse) in begin/rescue, validate i.link/i.id/i.title/i.content up front, and log per-item errors so a single bad entry does not poison the entire run.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that `i.content.scrub` raises when item content is nil, matching the golden comment's underlying bug. Although it broadens the discussion to other failures and recommends validation/rescue rather than a description fallback, it identifies the same missing-content crash.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer is interpolated into a JS context without j/JS escaping

`parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` relies on Rails default HTML escaping inside a JavaScript string literal. While `'` happens to be escaped in a way that is inert inside a `<script>` block today, the correct helper for a value going into a JS string literal is `j request.referer` (or escaping explicitly for targetOrigin). The embed controller deliberately lets attacker-controllable URLs reach the referer header, so passing that value to postMessage's targetOrigin should be JS-escaped so that backslashes/control bytes produced by a hostile header cannot break the JS string or smuggle a different targetOrigin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify request.referer being interpolated into a JavaScript string without proper JavaScript escaping, creating a risk from attacker-controlled header content. The candidate discusses additional targetOrigin implications but points to the same underlying escaping vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a recognized directive

The action unconditionally sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. The only valid X-Frame-Options values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN and the deprecated ALLOW-FROM <uri>. Browsers will silently ignore "ALLOWALL" and fall back to their default framing policy, so unless an equivalent Content-Security-Policy `frame-ancestors *` is set, the very framing that the embed feature was built to enable will be blocked in modern browsers. Use CSP `frame-ancestors *` (or remove this header and rely on CSP) instead.

feed_key helper is dead code

The class defines `feed_key` (computing `"feed-modified:#{Digest::SHA1.hexdigest(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)}"`) but never references it. Either wire it into the poll path (e.g., a per-feed HTTP If-Modified-Since/last-modified check, or a rate-limit key to avoid re-importing unchanged items) or remove the unused method to avoid the impression that per-feed change detection exists.

Throttle uses non-atomic SETNX + EXPIRE, which can leak a permanent key

`$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` leaves a brief window in which the key exists with no TTL. If the second command is lost (network blip, sidekiq preemption, Redis failover) the key has no expiry and permanently blocks retrievals for that URL. Use the atomic `SET key 1 NX EX 60` form instead.

TopicEmbed.import_remote (external URL fetch + ruby-readability) is not exercised

import_remote performs `open(url).read`, runs ruby-readability with the specific tags/attributes allowlist, and forwards the result into import. It is the highest-risk entry point in this PR (SSRF surface, hang on slow hosts, content that ends up as raw_html posts) and is reachable from both TopicRetriever#fetch_http and the disqus.thor import task. The new spec only covers import(), so any regression in the allowlist, the host contract, or the read/open behaviour would slip through.

poll_feed body (RSS item iteration, normalisation, TopicEmbed.import integration) is uncovered

The new spec only verifies the three guard conditions in execute() (feed_polling_enabled?, feed_polling_url present, embed_by_username present). The actual poll_feed body that parses the feed, falls back from i.link to i.id, runs CGI.unescapeHTML + i.content.scrub, and calls TopicEmbed.import per item is the section this review flagged as fragile (nil item fields, scrub failures, regex mismatch on id fallback) and is not tested at all.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate self.downsize method shadows earlier definition

Two class methods named self.downsize are defined back-to-back: one with signature (from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) on lines 145-147 and another with signature (from, to, dimensions, opts) on lines 149-151. In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first; the four-arg overload becomes dead code that is never reachable. The unused definition is misleading and will silently break any other caller that still passes separate width/height integers (those calls would now misroute 200 into the opts hash and raise NoMethodError on opts[:allow_animation]). The dead method should be deleted so only the (from, to, dimensions, opts) form remains.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the later dimensions-based signature overrides the earlier width/height signature, making it unreachable and breaking existing callers. The candidate's proposed fix and minor argument-count inaccuracies do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side file-size limit hardcoded to 10 MB and no longer uses SiteSettings

validateUploadedFile previously read `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` (and displayErrorForUpload read `SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`). The PR replaces both with a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. The server-side controller still uses `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb` (now with an auto-downsize step, but a server-enforced ceiling remains). This decouples client and server validation: an admin who lowers max_image_size_kb below 10 MB will see uploads rejected on the server with a generic 413, while the browser still claims files up to 10 MB are valid; raising max_image_size_kb above 10 MB will not relax the client-side cap. The previous site-setting based values should be restored, or the server limit should also be aligned with 10 MB.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the hardcoded 10 MB client-side limit replacing per-type SiteSettings values, causing divergence from server-configured limits. The candidate also covers the upload-error/413 handling noted in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Passing '80%' to gifsicle --resize-fit will fail for animated GIFs

The controller calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails). The animated branch in resize_instructions_animated assembles `gifsicle <from> --colors=256 --resize-fit 80% --optimize=3 --output <to>`. gifsicle's --resize-fit expects pixel dimensions of the form WxH; it does not accept a percentage. When allow_animated_thumbnails is enabled and the uploaded image is a GIF, this command will either be rejected by gifsicle or produce no useful output, so the downsize loop's exit-condition (tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes) will never become false and the GIF will be uploaded unmodified (and likely over the size limit).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: passing "80%" into the animated GIF path uses gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry rather than a percentage, causing downsizing to fail when animated thumbnails are enabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop does not verify the file is now within the size limit

The retry loop only checks `tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` before each iteration; if OptimizedImage.downsize returns false (e.g. convert/gifsicle fails, source is unsupported, or the file just can't be compressed enough at 80% scale for five attempts), the loop still exits with attempt reaching 0. The code then unconditionally calls Upload.create_for with `tempfile.size` and creates an Upload record whose underlying file exceeds SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. There is no fallback to reject the upload, no log line, and the user gets no error. The loop should re-check size after the downsize call (e.g. re-stat the file) and treat remaining-oversize as an error returned to the caller.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when TopicUser record does not exist

The unsubscribe action does `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and then unconditionally calls `tu.notification_level` and `tu.save!`. For any user who has not previously visited/read the topic (or whose topic_users row was deleted) there is no TopicUser row and `find_by` returns nil, so the first comparison raises NoMethodError on nil and the user sees a 500 instead of being unsubscribed. New users on a topic they have never opened will hit this on the very first click from the email. The action should use `TopicUser.find_or_create_by(...)` (or the existing `TopicUser.change` helper which already creates the row on miss) and otherwise guard against nil.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil, and unconditionally calling methods on it causes an exception.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Misspelled property leaks to template handlebars

The CP is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra 'i' after Notific). The template (`templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`) refers to it as `{{{stopNotificiationsText}}}` so it works, but the misspelling will bite anyone who tries to grep, rename, or reuse it, and Ember will warn about unknown handlebars bindings the moment either side is corrected. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` and update the template accordingly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the misspelled property 'stopNotificiationsText' and recommend renaming it to 'stopNotificationsText'. The candidate's additional template discussion does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate: GET-based state change with no auth token enables CSRF unsubscribe The unsubscribe endpoint is GET-only and the URL it generates (`{base}/t/{slug}/{id}/unsubscribe`) contains no per-user authentication token, unlike Discourse's other email-triggered endpoints (e.g. `email/unsubscribe/:key`, `users/password-reset/:token`, `users/activate-account/:token`). Any third-party site can force a logged-in Discourse user to be unsubscribed/muted from any topic simply by referencing the URL (e.g. as an ``, hidden link, or redirect). Once the user lands on it, `tu.save!` mutates their notification level with no confirm step. The action should either be POST/PUT (so Rails' CSRF token applies) or the link in the email should carry a signed/email-token like the existing global unsubscribe (`email#unsubscribe`) does.

No explicit guardian check before mutating state

Before doing `tu.save!` the controller relies on `TopicView.new` raising to deny access, but there is no explicit `guardian.ensure_can_see!(@topic_view.topic)` (or equivalent). If `TopicView.new` ever stops raising for some category/PM edge case, or if a later refactor changes that, the action will happily downgrade a TopicUser row for a topic the user is not entitled to interact with. Add an explicit guardian check (matching the pattern used by `clear_pin`/`re_pin`/`mute` in the same controller) before mutating user state.

mailing_list_notify omits unsubscribe_url, breaking the feature for mailing-list users

`send_notification_email` is shared between the per-user notification path and `mailing_list_notify`, but `mailing_list_notify` (lines 146-159) builds its opts hash without `unsubscribe_url:` while the other callers now pass `unsubscribe_url: post.topic.unsubscribe_url`. As a result users in mailing-list mode still get the old footer with only the global preferences link and no per-topic unsubscribe link, which is inconsistent with the stated goal of this PR and means the new i18n text "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})" is never shown for these emails.

New unsubscribe behavior is not actually asserted

The diff only adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the existing `message_with_unsubscribe` let-block, but no expectation is added that this URL ends up in the rendered body. The "unsubscribe link" context only checks that the user preferences URL appears; there is no test asserting that `unsubscribe_url` is interpolated into the `unsubscribe_link` i18n key and surfaces in the body/html_part. Given the i18n string was changed and the unsubscribe_url plumbing is brand new, a regression here would silently produce emails with the global-preferences-only footer again.

No controller spec for the new unsubscribe action

There is no topics_controller_spec coverage for the new `unsubscribe` action: nil-TopicUser case, slug mismatch redirect, the regular->muted vs tracking/watching->regular branch, permission denial, and that the rendered view is `topics/show`. Combined with the silent `tu.save!` and the fact that this action is the entry point for every per-topic unsubscribe email, a regression here will only be caught in production.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data, likely throws PrismaClientValidationError

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` ends with `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` and the comment says it is meant to bump `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`. The Prisma client rejects empty `data` objects for updateMany ("data must have at least one non-relation field"), so this call will throw at runtime. Because this method runs inside the `unwatchCalendar` flow (only when there are remaining calendars), the throw will leave the unwatch in a half-completed state and the `remainingCalendars` cache will be re-fetched before updatedAt is updated — or, more likely, the user receives a confusing error from the webhook flow. Either pass a real column (e.g. `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`) or stop calling this and rely on the existing cache-write side effects.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the empty data object in updateManyByCredentialId as preventing the intended updatedAt refresh and suggest explicitly setting updatedAt. The candidate incorrectly attributes the failure to a Prisma validation error, but points to the same problematic call and underlying timestamp-update concern.

false_positives.candidate:
getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt and returns data for stale cache

The query groups by credentialId and takes the max updatedAt, but never filters by `expiresAt`. A `CalendarCache` row whose `expiresAt` is in the past will not be served by `getCachedAvailability` (which uses `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }`), yet the new UI in `CredentialActionsDropdown` will still display "Cache Status: Last updated …" for that credential. Users will see a cache status indicator for cache that is effectively dead. Either add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` to the `where` clause, or surface the cache only when not expired.

No tests cover deleteCache tRPC mutation, getCacheStatusByCredentialIds, or the new component

The new `viewer.calendars.deleteCache` tRPC mutation, the new `CalendarCacheRepository.getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` method (including its mock), and the entire `CredentialActionsDropdown` component (including the access-control conditional rendering for delegation credentials and disabled connections) have no unit or integration tests. This PR also adds a security-relevant authorization check (`userId: user.id` in `deleteCache.handler.ts`); a regression that drops that check would be silent without a test. Add at minimum: a test that `deleteCacheHandler` rejects a credential belonging to another user, a test that `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` filters/doesn't filter expiresAt as intended, and a render test for the component's conditional dropdown rendering.

Removes type-check on findMany args and over-widens updateManyByCredentialId

Two changes to this file: (1) the change at line ~260 removes the `satisfies Prisma.SelectedCalendarFindManyArgs` so callers can now pass an object that is structurally invalid for Prisma (e.g. misspelled keys) and the compiler will no longer flag it. That weakens a type-safety net that was deliberately added with `satisfies`. (2) `updateManyByCredentialId` accepts `data: Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` with no constraint enforcing non-empty `data`, which is exactly how the empty-`{}` bug at `CalendarService.ts:1024` slipped in. Tighten the parameter type to a non-empty variant (e.g. a branded `AtLeastOne<Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput>`) and consider restoring the `satisfies`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
checkIfIsAvailable workingHours check has duplicated start/end computation

Inside checkIfIsAvailable the new workingHours branch computes `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` and then `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` -- both variables are identical (copy-paste of the same expression). The subsequent guard `if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime)` therefore only checks the slot's start time against both bounds and never validates that the slot actually fits inside the working window. A slot starting 30 minutes before the configured end of the working hours (e.g. start 17:30 with workingHour.endTime 18:00 and eventLength 60) would be wrongly accepted. To check whether the slot fits, `end` must be the slot end (slotStartTime + eventLength) or the comparison must be expressed as `slotEnd > workingHour.endTime`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the end time is computed from slotStartTime rather than slotEndTime, causing the availability check to miss slots that extend beyond working hours.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the round-robin fixed-host date-override fix

The PR description states the primary bug fix is that 'date overrides of fixed hosts are taken into account for round-robin events' (Fixes #8207, #8273). The only test added (lines 786-804) re-runs the existing personal-event 'Check for Date overrides' scenario with a different invitee timezone. There is no test that creates a round-robin event with a fixed host, adds a date override for that fixed host, and asserts that the returned slots are restricted to the fixed host's override. Without such a test the main advertised fix is unverified and could regress silently.

checkIfIsAvailable mixes UTC and local timezones when matching override date to slot date

`slotStartTime = time.utc()` (UTC) is compared via `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')`. The other side, `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')`, uses `dayjs(date.start)` (parsed in the server's local timezone) plus an offset, and then formats in the server's local timezone. On any server whose local timezone is not the same as `organizerTimeZone` (or UTC) the two formatted dates can disagree for slots at the boundary of a day, causing date overrides to be ignored or applied to the wrong day. Both sides must be normalized to the same timezone (e.g. `dayjs.utc(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on the left, and `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format(...)` on the right).

checkIfIsAvailable uses side effects inside Array.find and only honors the first matching date override

The new code reuses `Array.prototype.find` to set the outer `dateOverrideExist` flag as a side effect while also using its return value to decide whether the slot is inside the override. As soon as the first matching override returns `true` (slot outside that override), the remaining overrides are skipped. For a user with several date overrides on the same day (e.g. one morning, one afternoon) only the first is consulted, so a slot that lies inside the second override but outside the first is wrongly classified. The mutation of `dateOverrideExist` from inside `find` is also fragile and easy to break in future refactors. The override matching should be written as an explicit loop or `Array#some`/`every` without mutating shared state.

checkIfIsAvailable compares day/hour/minute in UTC against organizer's working hours

`slotStartTime = time.utc()` puts the slot in UTC, so `slotStartTime.day()`, `slotStartTime.hour()` and `slotStartTime.minute()` return UTC values. The `workingHour` records, however, are expressed in the organizer's timezone (their `days` array and `startTime`/`endTime` in minutes since organizer-local midnight). With any non-zero UTC offset this check is wrong: e.g. an organizer in IST with working hours 09:30-18:00 IST would see a slot at 04:30 UTC (=10:00 IST, inside working hours) produce UTC day/hour = previous-day/04, which does not match `workingHour.days.includes(...)` and `start < workingHour.startTime` is false but the wrong-day branch will be exercised. The slot must be converted to organizerTimeZone (`slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone)`) before reading day/hour/minute.

Date override offset uses Date.toString() and reparses in the server's local timezone

The new override offset calculation is `const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();`. `override.start` is already a Date; calling `.toString()` produces a locale-dependent representation which dayjs then parses using the server's local timezone. On a server whose local timezone is not UTC this shifts the underlying moment in time, and consequently the `utcOffset()` (which depends on the moment, e.g. across DST boundaries) can be computed at the wrong instant. The same pattern is used for `inviteeUtcOffset`. Use the Date directly: `dayjs(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` (or `dayjs.utc(override.start).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` to be unambiguous).

dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, ...) computed four times per entry

The new override branch evaluates `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` twice and the equivalent expression for `override.end` twice (lines 219-223). With many overrides per day this multiplies the cost unnecessarily and also makes the four expressions easy to drift out of sync in future edits. Compute each adjusted moment once and reuse it for both `.hour()`/`.minute()` and the equality check.

Strict-equality on dayjs objects depends on undocumented valueOf

The new date-override zero-length guard uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')`. Two freshly constructed dayjs instances are never `===` unless their `valueOf()` (millisecond timestamp) is equal, which is true here only because dayjs forwards valueOf to the underlying timestamp. This works but is non-obvious and breaks if dayjs is ever replaced or if `add` introduces sub-millisecond precision differences. Use `.isSame(other, ...)` or compare `valueOf()` explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Find-then-update is not atomic; concurrent cron ticks can double-schedule and double-count retries

The handler does `findMany({ scheduled: false })` and then, in a separate loop, calls `twilio.scheduleSMS` and finally updates `scheduled = true` (or `retryCount += 1`). There is no transaction, row lock, or `update ... where { scheduled: false } returning ...` guard, so if two cron invocations overlap (or the previous run is retried while still in flight) both will fetch the same `scheduled: false` row and both will call Twilio, producing two scheduled SMS messages for the same reminder. The new retryCount increment makes the failure path worse: if Twilio throws, both concurrent handlers hit the catch block and both write `retryCount: N + 1`, so retryCount can be undercounted (e.g. two simultaneous failures on a row at retryCount=0 both write 1 instead of 2) and the row may survive an extra round instead of being deleted. This should be made atomic, e.g. by doing an `updateMany` with `where: { id, scheduled: false }` returning the row, or by wrapping the scheduling call in a transaction with a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies concurrent writes of retryCount: N + 1 losing increments and undercounting retries, which is the same stale-read race described by the golden comment. Its additional double-scheduling concern and different proposed fix do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup not scoped to SMS method

The new deleteMany adds an OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` that has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, while the sibling branch does. Today only this SMS handler ever increments `retryCount`, so only SMS rows are affected in practice — but the column is on the general `WorkflowReminder` model and the migration defaults all rows to 0. As soon as any other path (a future EMAIL/WHATSAPP scheduler, a backfill, an admin tool, manual SQL) sets `retryCount` on a non-SMS reminder, this query will silently delete those rows along with the SMS ones. The branch should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (or the second OR arm should be merged into the first with `AND`) so the cleanup cannot reach reminders of other methods.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion branch, which permits deletion of non-SMS reminders. The candidate's qualification about current usage does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Permanent SMS drops after retry exhaustion are silent

When a reminder crosses `retryCount > 1` it is deleted by the next cron tick with no log line and no notification. The catch path only logs the underlying `twilio.scheduleSMS` error; once the row is later deleted by the `retryCount > 1` branch there is no trace that the user was supposed to receive an SMS at all. Given this is precisely the case the PR is trying to surface ("after scheduling failed twice we delete"), the deleteMany should at minimum log the reminder id, booking uid, workflowStep, and last error so that the dropped reminders are visible in logs and can be alerted on or surfaced to the organizer.

Public findMany method removed; callers must adopt getBaseConditions + $queryRaw

The diff replaces the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. The new method only returns a WHERE-clause SQL fragment; callers must now embed it in their own `prisma.$queryRaw` template and write the SELECT themselves. Any existing consumer of the service (e.g. insights API endpoints or other internal callers that previously did `service.findMany({ select: { ... } })`) will break: the method is gone, so those calls become a runtime TypeError, not just a behavior change. The PR description frames this as a test-only update and never mentions the contract change, nor does it list which callers were migrated, so it is unclear whether every callsite has been updated in lockstep.

Caching behavior of getAuthorizationConditions/getFilterConditions is no longer tested

The diff deletes the entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block, which previously contained `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions`. The service still implements caching in `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions` (`if (this.cachedAuthConditions === undefined) { this.cachedAuthConditions = await this.buildAuthorizationConditions(); }`), but no test now exercises that branch. A future regression that accidentally rebuilds the conditions on every call would re-run the membership/team queries on every request and degrade performance without any test catching it. The caching tests should be re-added in the new `Prisma.sql` comparison style rather than dropped entirely.

This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
parseRefreshTokenResponse writes literal 'refresh_token' string into saved credentials

When `refresh_token` is missing from the parsed response the function does `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`, mutating the parsed object. Callers then persist this object back into the Credential row (see googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:97-101, office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:263-273 which spreads tokenResponse.data over o365AuthCredentials). The literal string "refresh_token" is saved as the OAuth refresh token. The next refresh attempt will send that string to Google/Microsoft/etc. and fail, and users have no way to recover without manually editing the DB. The function should either leave refresh_token alone (and let the caller decide what to do) or reject the response as invalid.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse substitutes the literal string 'refresh_token' when the response omits a refresh token, resulting in an invalid token and failed subsequent refreshes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema's dynamic keys are no-ops in Zod

`z.object({ [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })` does not do what the comments claim. The bracketed expressions are evaluated once at schema creation time and resolve to the string `"ZodString"` (or similar), so this is effectively a single extra key "ZodString" on the object. It does not enforce "any property with a number is the expiry" nor does it allow arbitrary additional properties. When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true the schema only requires `access_token` to be a string and otherwise accepts anything, so invalid/garbage token responses from the parent app will pass validation and be written into Cal.com's Credential table.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the computed Zod schema keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema as the underlying bug. Although the candidate describes ineffective validation rather than a runtime error, it points to the same misuse of z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() as property keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
refreshOAuthTokens returns incompatible types based on sync flag

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, this function calls fetch(...) and returns the fetch Response object. Otherwise it returns whatever refreshFunction() returns (which is provider-specific: a GaxiosResponse for googlecalendar, a HubspotToken for hubspot, an AxiosResponse for zoho-bigin/zohocrm, a fetch Response for office365calendar/office365video/webex/zoomvideo/larkcalendar). Whenever the sync flag is enabled, these integrations will throw at runtime and break OAuth flows. The function must either always return a normalized shape (e.g. parsed JSON) or be split into two functions so callers know which shape they get.

The candidate adds examples and remediation without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce refresh check uses response.statusText !== 'OK' which is unreliable

`if (response.statusText !== "OK")` rejects any response whose status text differs from "OK". Many proxies / HTTP/2 responses return an empty statusText, and `response.ok` is the documented boolean for status 200-299. As written, a successful 200 refresh with an empty statusText will throw `HttpError(statusCode: 400, message: '')` and the credential will not be updated. Use `if (!response.ok)` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the Salesforce OAuth refresh bug of checking response.statusText instead of response.ok, which can misclassify successful responses and prevent credentials from being updated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce Connection is built from the expired access token, not the freshly refreshed one

After the new refresh block saves `{...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token}` to the DB, the immediately-following `new jsforce.Connection({ ... accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` still passes the OLD access token from `credentialKey`. The connection is therefore used with the token that was just deemed expired enough to refresh. Salesforce API calls will be made with a stale token until the next request re-reads the credential from the DB, causing intermittent auth failures for bookings and contacts sync. Should be `accessToken: accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: jsforce.Connection uses stale credential values after a token refresh instead of the refreshed values. Although it does not mention the stale instance_url, it correctly identifies the stale access token and resulting authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method, including GET

The handler performs no `req.method` check, meaning GET, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc. all flow through the same code path and are capable of creating or updating credentials. This makes CSRF-style attacks and accidental re-triggering via browser prefetch / link previews much easier. Add an explicit check that the request method is POST (or whatever the documented method is) and return 405 otherwise.

Webhook secret compared with !==, vulnerable to timing attack

The secret check uses `req.headers[name] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. String equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so an attacker with request-latency measurement capability (e.g. colocated on the same cloud region) can recover the secret byte-by-byte. Use a constant-time comparison such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(headerValue), Buffer.from(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET))` after length-checking.

Find-then-create/update is racy and will produce duplicate credentials

Between the `prisma.credential.findFirst` on line 62 and the subsequent `prisma.credential.create` on line 83 there is no transaction or unique constraint covering (userId, appId). Two near-simultaneous webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appSlug) will both observe no existing credential and both create one, producing duplicate credentials that later code paths (which use `findFirst`) silently ignore while the orphan still consumes app quota / shows in admin UIs. Use a single `prisma.credential.upsert` with a where clause on `(userId, appId)`, or wrap in `$transaction` with the proper unique constraint.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` is typed as `string | undefined` and the runtime value is either the second operand's string or the empty/falsy string `""` for the first operand. The codebase then uses `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED) { return 403 }` and `if (APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && ...)`. This works for the obvious cases but silently treats the literal string `"false"` as truthy, and is fragile if either env var is ever set to a non-empty placeholder. Coerce with `!!` (or compare against empty string) and ideally name it like a boolean.

Decrypt/JSON.parse failures are not caught

`symmetricDecrypt(...)` will throw if CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is missing (the `|| ""` fallback produces an unusable key), and `JSON.parse` will throw on any non-JSON plaintext. Because this happens after the secret check, an unauthenticated-bypass-shaped input becomes an unhandled 500 (and in some Next.js handler configs may leak stack info). Wrap the decrypt + parse in try/catch and return 400 with a non-leaky message; also early-return 503 when CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is unset.

redirectUri hardcodes 'zoho-bigin' instead of appConfig.slug

The diff replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``. If appConfig.slug ever changes or the file is copied for another app, this diverges from the rest of the file (which still uses appConfig.slug elsewhere). Either keep using `appConfig.slug` or extract a constant.

turbo.json lists CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY before CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET, breaking alphabetical order

Minor: in the new globalEnv block, `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is added on line 205, then `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` on 206, then `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` on 207. The surrounding block was previously alphabetical (CALCOM_ENV, CALCOM_LICENSE_KEY, CALCOM_TELEMETRY_DISABLED, CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, CI). The new entries are inserted out of order, which makes future diffs and merges noisier without affecting behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget (no await)

The loop at lines 485-493 calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` inside `forEach` but never awaits the returned promises. The handler then continues and returns a 'Booking successfully cancelled' response while Twilio cancellation and the `cancelled: true` DB update may still be pending. A failing Twilio/SendGrid call or DB write is silently dropped, the DB may still read `scheduled: true`, and the CRON will not see the cancellation. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `Promise.all(updatedBookings.flatMap(...))`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: asynchronous reminder deletion functions are invoked inside forEach without awaiting their promises, allowing booking cancellation to finish before scheduled reminders are reliably cancelled. Although it discusses only booking cancellation rather than all affected workflows, it matches the core bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves DB row unchanged

When `immediateDelete=true`, the function only posts to SendGrid and returns without touching the database. The `WorkflowReminder` row remains with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled` unset. If the SendGrid cancel call fails (e.g. transient error or the historic 100-cancellation limit), there is no record of the attempt and the row will not be retried by the CRON (which only looks at `cancelled: true`). The row will only be cleaned up after `scheduledDate` passes. Set `cancelled: true` (or delete the row) on this path as well, so failures are recoverable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the immediateDelete=true path cancels through SendGrid without updating or deleting the WorkflowReminder database record, leaving an orphaned or unchanged row. The candidate does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, but it matches the core database-state bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration adds nullable column without NOT NULL or default

The migration is `ALTER TABLE "WorkflowReminder" ADD COLUMN "cancelled" BOOLEAN;` — no NOT NULL, no DEFAULT. For new rows the application always writes a value, so this is fine in practice, but it makes the schema's intent ambiguous. Either add `NOT NULL DEFAULT false` (preferred; all existing rows become `false`) or document that `NULL` means 'not cancelled' explicitly in the migration comment.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the cancelled column is nullable and lacks a default, leaving existing records with NULL rather than false. Although the candidate downplays the behavioral impact, it identifies the same schema issue and proposes NOT NULL DEFAULT false.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminder cancellation in requestReschedule is fire-and-forget

`bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited. The trpc mutation then proceeds to send emails, update DB, delete refs, etc., and finally returns before the SendGrid/Twilio cancellation has completed (or even started). Failures are not propagated. Should be a `for...of` loop with `await`, or collect and `Promise.all`.

Reminder cancellation in workflow delete is fire-and-forget

`scheduledReminders.forEach(...)` returns promises that are never awaited before `ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` runs. The workflow delete cascades through `WorkflowStep` and may delete the `WorkflowReminder` rows (via onDelete: Cascade) before SendGrid/Twilio cancellation completes, leaving third-party systems with still-scheduled sends and no DB record to retry. Await the cancellations before deleting the workflow.

Reminder cancellation for disabled event types is fire-and-forget

The `remindersToDelete.flat().forEach(...)` block calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting. These are then followed by further awaits like `prisma.workflowsOnEventTypes.deleteMany`, so the mutation returns before cancellations complete and any error is silently swallowed.

Reminder cancellation on step edit is fire-and-forget

`remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => {...})` does not await. The mutation continues and returns while SendGrid/Twilio cancellations may still be in flight. Errors are silently swallowed. Await the operations.

unscheduledReminders query ignores the new cancelled flag

The query that picks up `scheduled: false` reminders to push to SendGrid does not filter on `cancelled`. When a booking is cancelled more than 72 hours before a reminder fires, the reminder row has `cancelled: true` but `scheduled: false`. The next CRON run within 72h of `scheduledDate` will still schedule it via SendGrid. The CRON will subsequently try to cancel the resulting SendGrid send in its 1-hour window, but this is wasteful at best and creates a window in which the email is queued. Add `cancelled: { not: true }` (or `cancelled: false`) to the `where` filter on line 82-87.

Cancel loop awaits SendGrid calls sequentially

Inside `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` each iteration awaits a SendGrid HTTP call before moving on. With any non-trivial number of cancellations this serialises the network round-trips (CRON has a hard 15-min cadence and other tenants share it). Use `Promise.allSettled` (or chunked parallel batches) so a single failed call doesn't abort the others and so throughput is reasonable.

1-hour cancel window leaves reminders scheduled in SendGrid

`remindersToCancel` only matches `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Reminders that were already pushed to SendGrid and whose `scheduledDate` is between 1 and 72 hours away are silently skipped: they remain as pending sends in SendGrid. If the CRON is delayed beyond the 1-hour buffer (which it can be, given that it runs every 15 minutes and can be throttled), SendGrid will deliver a reminder for a booking that was cancelled or rescheduled — the same bug this PR is meant to fix. Either cancel in SendGrid immediately on the cancel/reschedule path, or process all `cancelled: true` reminders in this loop, not just the next hour.

Signature change of deleteScheduledEmailReminder is inconsistent across the codebase

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` now requires a `reminderId: number` as the first parameter. Existing callers were updated, but the parameter order (id before referenceId) is unusual since the function historically only needed the external reference. Consider reordering to `(referenceId, reminderId, immediateDelete)` to match `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`'s spirit (which keeps referenceId first) and to minimise future misuse.

SMS cancellation deletes the DB row even when Twilio cancel fails

`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` first calls `twilio.cancelSMS(referenceId)` and then unconditionally deletes the DB row, all inside the same `try`. If Twilio throws, the catch logs and returns, but the SMS may still be queued at Twilio and there is no record to retry. The flow for email intentionally defers cancellation to a CRON-style mechanism for resilience; the SMS path has no equivalent. Either mirror the email design (`cancelled: true` + CRON) or move the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` outside the try so the delete only happens on Twilio success.

Verification-code TextField is not bound to form state

In the phone-number verification UI, `TextField` for the verification code uses a local `verificationCode` state via `onChange`, but is rendered with `value={verificationCode}` and no `name` registration. The field shows correctly while mounted, but loses its value if the component remounts (e.g. switching action types triggers `setNumberVerified(false)` and `setIsPhoneNumberNeeded(...)` re-renders). It also leaks `verificationCode` between steps because it is component-level state, not scoped to `step.stepNumber`. The original layout (before this PR's refactor) had the same code, but since the panel was hoisted into its own block here, multiple steps now share the same single state variable.

Step-deletion cancellations are fire-and-forget before prisma.workflowStep.delete

`remindersFromStep.forEach(reminder => deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...))` is not awaited before `prisma.workflowStep.delete({ where: { id: oldStep.id } })`. Because `WorkflowStep` has `onDelete: Cascade` on `WorkflowReminder`, the delete will remove the reminder rows from the DB before SendGrid/Twilio has had a chance to cancel them, leaving third-party queues with pending sends. Await the cancellations first.

Past-reminder cleanup deletes rows before SendGrid actually fires

The first action of the CRON deletes every `WorkflowReminder` row whose `scheduledDate <= now`. This is supposed to be housekeeping for already-sent reminders, but the only signal that an email was actually delivered is the row's existence. If SendGrid is delayed or the CRON runs late, reminders that have not been sent yet can be deleted from the DB while still being queued in SendGrid, leading to silent drops. Track delivery status (or only delete `cancelled: true` past reminders) rather than every past-scheduled row.

No tests added for the cancellation fix

This PR changes the data flow for cancelling workflow reminders on booking cancel/reschedule and adds a new DB column plus a new CRON path. There are no tests covering: (a) that `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` sets `cancelled: true` correctly, (b) that the CRON only processes `cancelled: true` rows within the window, (c) that reschedule/reschedule-via-trpc paths actually cancel, or (d) regression coverage for the bug in #7225. The previous attempt also broke things; without tests the same risk exists here.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Case-sensitive blacklist and existing-attendee filter are trivially bypassable

All email comparisons for guest handling should be lowercased before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner permission check uses && instead of ||

The `isTeamAdminOrOwner` check uses `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. In cal.com's role model these are mutually exclusive (a user is either admin OR owner), so the conjunction always evaluates to false. The code clearly intended `||`. Effect: every team admin and every team owner is treated as unauthorized and rejected with `FORBIDDEN`; only direct organizers or existing attendees can add guests to team event bookings, defeating the entire intent of this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same permission-check bug: using && requires a user to be both a team admin and owner, whereas || should allow either role.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails is called with unfiltered input, causing duplicate AttendeeScheduledEmail to existing attendees

The handler passes the original `guests` array (which may contain already-attending emails that were filtered out into `uniqueGuests`) into `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`. In `email-manager.ts` the attendees loop then does `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` and sends `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (the standard 'you have been booked' email, full calendar invite) to any existing attendee whose email happens to be in the raw input. If an organizer re-typings an existing attendee's email by mistake, that attendee will be re-issued a brand-new booking confirmation with a fresh ICS REQUEST. The function should receive the deduplicated `uniqueGuests` (or compute the post-update set) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same classification bug: sendAddGuestsEmails iterates over all calendarEvent.attendees and checks membership in the raw input guests array, potentially sending AttendeeScheduledEmail to existing attendees rather than AttendeeAddGuestsEmail.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing attendees are allowed to add arbitrary guests

Permission check is `!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee -> FORBIDDEN`. Because `isAttendee` is satisfied by any existing attendee whose email matches the logged-in user's email, an invitee of a booking can invite unlimited additional people (including themselves under a different email) to that booking without the organizer's consent. This is a privilege escalation: an attendee can grow the meeting's attendee list and trigger calendar invites / emails on behalf of the organizer. At minimum, only the organizer / team admin / owner should be able to add guests.

No booking status check: guests can be added to cancelled or past bookings

The handler never inspects `booking.status` (or `booking.startTime`). The action item in `BookingListItem.tsx` is reachable for past confirmed bookings and any tRPC caller can bypass the UI entirely and call the mutation for a cancelled/rejected booking. Adding attendees to a cancelled booking results in an orphan calendar invite to a meeting that will not occur and may push the meeting back into an active state on connected calendars.

Calendar sync after DB commit with no rollback: inconsistent state on failure

`prisma.booking.update` is executed before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. The calendar update is not wrapped in try/catch, so if it throws (e.g. credentials revoked, Google 5xx) the DB rows have already been inserted but the connected calendar has not been updated. A retry will then hit `uniqueGuests.length === 0` and return a misleading `emails_must_be_unique_valid` error, leaving the meeting with attendees in the DB but not on the calendar and not notified. The handler should either perform the calendar update first (with compensation on DB failure) or wrap both in a transactional pattern.

EventManager is built from the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

`new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` uses the currently authenticated user's spread and credentials. The booking's actual organizer is loaded into `organizer` but its credentials are not used. When the caller is a team admin or (in the corrected logic) an attendee, the calendar invite will be pushed through whichever calendar integration the caller has, not the organizer's. That causes the organizer to lose control of the event on their primary calendar and may fail entirely if the caller has no calendar credentials for the destinationCalendar.

No upper bound on guests array: trivially exploitable DoS / cost amplification

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max(...)`. A single authed user can submit an array of thousands of valid emails. The handler then performs N inserts, N `getTranslation` calls, one big `Promise.all` of N emails, and a calendar update with an attendees list of size N. There is no per-user / per-booking throttle. A reasonable bound (e.g. `.max(50)` or `.max(100)`) should be enforced at the schema layer to prevent abuse and keep the email/calendar blast radius small.

findFirst -> filter -> update pattern has a TOCTOU race that can create duplicate attendees

The handler reads `booking.attendees` and then issues `prisma.booking.update` with `attendees.createMany`. Between those two statements another request from the same organizer can insert the same guest; because there is no unique index on (bookingId, email) and no transactional check, both requests will succeed and produce duplicate attendee rows that share the same email on the same booking. The de-duplication should be done inside a single transaction (or use a unique constraint) to make the operation atomic.

New-guest check is performed after formatCalEvent, mixing raw input with formatted attendees

`calendarEvent.attendees` is the formatted list returned from `formatCalEvent(calEvent)`, but `newGuests` is the raw caller-supplied array. If `formatCalEvent` normalizes email casing (or trims/strips display-name suffixes), `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` will silently mis-classify a new guest as an existing attendee (or vice-versa), causing the wrong email template to be sent. Both sides of the comparison must go through the same normalization.

Email To header uses empty name for newly-added guests and can crash senders

`to: `${this.attendee.name} <${this.attendee.email}>`` is built unconditionally. The handler inserts new attendees with `name: ""` (`addGuests.handler.ts:85`), so every new-guest email is addressed as ` <new@example.com>`, which most SMTP servers reject as malformed. New guests should have a name populated (or the formatter should fall back to the local part of the email).

Subject reads attendees[0].name without guarding empty array

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` if `attendees` is empty (e.g. an organizer-only booking or a booking whose attendees were wiped before this code path runs). It also produces a blank name in the subject for any new-guest-led booking where the first attendee was inserted with `name: ""`.

Inline Zod schema diverges from the backend schema and validates case-sensitively

The dialog defines its own `z.array(z.string().email()).refine(... set uniqueness ...)` which is case-sensitive (`Set('A@x')` and `Set('a@x')` are different keys) and duplicates the rules from `addGuests.schema.ts`. If the two schemas drift, the user sees a confusing 'Emails must be unique and valid' error even when only one specific field is empty/invalid, and the backend may accept what the frontend rejected. The schema should live in a shared module and lower-case emails before the uniqueness check.

User-facing error toast prefixes the tRPC error code and raw translation key

`showToast(`${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, 'error')` exposes internal codes like `BAD_REQUEST: booking_not_found` (because `booking_not_found` is not present in the locale file, so `t()` returns the raw key) directly to end users. The fallback `t("unable_to_add_guests")` is only reached when the constructed string is falsy, which it never is. The toast should display the translated message and use the generic fallback when translation is missing.

Returns a hard-coded English success message instead of the i18n key

The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`. Other handlers in this router return translation keys (e.g. `booking_confirmation_success`) that the client renders via `t()`. Returning an English string here breaks localization and the toast on success (`t("guests_added")`) is wired separately, so the API contract is inconsistent with the rest of the bookings router.

No tests added for a new mutating handler that touches DB, calendar and email

The handler introduces an end-to-end flow with multiple non-trivial branches: permission check (organizer / attendee / team admin / team owner, including the && vs || bug above), blacklist filtering, duplicate attendee detection across casing, calendar sync ordering, and email dispatch for organizer / team members / new guests / existing attendees. None of these paths are exercised by tests in this PR. Given the security-sensitive nature of the changes (any authed user can mutate a booking's attendee list), at least the permission branches, status guard (once added), and the `sendAddGuestsEmails` recipient classification must be covered.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition lets a backup code be reused

The backup-code consumption path in authorize() reads user.backupCodes, decrypts it with JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)), nulls the matched slot, re-encrypts, and writes the result back via prisma.user.update with no atomicity guard. Two concurrent requests submitting different valid backup codes both read the same pre-image, each null a different index in their local copy, and whichever update commits last overwrites the other writer's null — restoring the slot the first request consumed. Consequence: a backup code can be used more than once, breaking the one-time-use guarantee the PR explicitly relies on (see the comment 'delete verified backup code and re-encrypt remaining'). Fix by making the update atomic, e.g. wrap read+write in prisma.$transaction, or include the expected pre-image in the WHERE clause so the second writer is rejected.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same non-atomic read-modify-write race in backup-code consumption, allowing codes to be accepted more than once. The candidate describes concurrent use of different codes causing a lost update, while the golden describes concurrent use of the same code; both stem from the same missing concurrency guard and violate one-time-use semantics.

In a collective event whose first destination belongs to a Google host, Lark will be asked to create the event under that Google external id and the request will fail or write to the wrong calendar.

Same pattern as Lark: the new Calendar interface and EventManager pass `credentialId` and `destination.externalId`, but Office365's implementation just takes `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. teamDestinationCalendars pushed without dedup; can create duplicate events on same calendar

Hosts that share a single connected destination calendar (a common case when multiple members point at the same Google account) will each contribute the same entry, leading EventManager.create to call `createEvent` twice for the same calendar+credential and create duplicate events in that calendar.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async) fire-and-forget on calendar/video deletions

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` discards the returned promises. The surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { ... }` cannot catch rejections from inside the async callback, and the caller (reschedule API) returns to the user once the synchronous portion of the loop ends. As a result, calendar `deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` calls may still be in flight when the function returns `true` and the reschedule email is sent, leading to inconsistent state (booking marked rescheduled while old events are not yet deleted). This was made worse by the async conversion because both `getCalendar` and the deletion calls are now Promise-returning; before, only `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` were promise-returning. Replace with `for (const bookingRef of bookingRefsFiltered)` and `await` each step, or build an array of promises and `await Promise.all(...)`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same async forEach bug: callback promises are discarded, operations run without being awaited, surrounding try-catch cannot catch their rejections, and cleanup may remain incomplete when the function returns. It also recommends the same fixes: awaited for...of loops or Promise.all with mapped promises.

false_positives.candidate:
forEach(async) fire-and-forget on calendar/video deletions

Identical issue to `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts:125`. The async `forEach` callback's promises are dropped, so `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls may not complete (and rejections are uncaught) before this function returns `true` and the reschedule flow continues. Replace with a sequential `for ... of` loop or `Promise.all(...)` over the references.

forEach(async) on calendar/video deletions in requestReschedule

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the returned promises. The function falls straight through to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and the rest of the mutation while the calendar `deleteEvent` and `deleteMeeting` calls are still pending. There is no `try/catch` around the loop either, so any rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection. With the new async `getCalendar`, the call now performs a lazy chunk download for every credential in addition to the network call to the provider, making the race more likely to be observed. Convert to `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` or a sequential `for ... of` with awaited steps.

forEach(async) on recurring-event calendar deletions

In the recurring-event branch of cancellation, `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { ... })` discards the returned promises, so the function reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and returns the HTTP response before the per-credential calendar deletions have finished. The outer `try/catch` does not cover this loop either. Because `getCalendar` is now async, this serializes per-credential dynamic chunk loads behind an unawaited loop, widening the race window. Replace with a proper loop that collects promises and lets `Promise.all` drive completion.

Resolved value pushed to apiDeletes instead of the promise

Inside the unawaited forEach above, `const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent);` pushes the already-resolved value (or `undefined`) into `apiDeletes` rather than the pending Promise. The later `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` therefore never waits for those deleteEvent calls in the recurring-event path (and even if forEach were fixed to await, the push would still capture resolved values). Push the Promise returned by `deleteEvent` directly, i.e. `apiDeletes.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId) as Promise<unknown> | undefined);` and let `Promise.all` await it.

getVideoAdapters serializes dynamic imports

The previous `reduce` implementation ran the entire synchronous mapping in one pass; the new implementation uses a sequential `for (const cred of withCredentials) { const app = await appStore[...]; ... }`, so every credential now blocks the next on its dynamic import + module evaluation. With multiple video credentials attached (Zoom, Daily, Whereby, etc.) this turns into N sequential async chunks where it used to be one synchronous pass and could be N parallel `Promise.all(creds.map(...))` calls. Replace with `Promise.all(withCredentials.map(...))` to keep the parallel cost similar to before.

getCalendarCredentials is sync but leaks Promise<Calendar> in its result

`getCalendarCredentials` was kept synchronous, yet inside it `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>` because `getCalendar` became async. The returned objects therefore carry `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>`, but the function signature does not advertise that and callers must remember to `await item.calendar` (which is exactly what the new `getConnectedCalendars` body now has to do). Either make `getCalendarCredentials` async and `await getCalendar`, or stop calling `getCalendar` inside it and only return `{ integration, credential }`, leaving adapter construction to the caller. As written, the public type lies about its return value and any future caller that treats `item.calendar` as a sync `Calendar` will get a rejected promise.

Awaiting already-resolved apiDeletes entries in seat cancellation

After `Promise.all(integrationsToDelete).then(async () => { ... })` resolves, the code schedules `prisma.booking.update` for last-attendee seat cancellation, but `integrationsToDelete` was built by `await getCalendar(credential); integrationsToDelete.push(calendar?.deleteEvent(...))`. Since `deleteEvent` is not awaited here, the pushed value is the unresolved Promise, which is correct. However this pattern is mixed with the broken recurring-event branch (see the other findings on lines 460/466), and the inconsistency makes the file easy to misread. After fixing the recurring branch, ensure the whole file consistently pushes pending Promises into the arrays that `Promise.all` later drains, instead of awaiting-then-pushing.
