false_positives.candidate:
Lithuanian translation replaced with Italian text

The `loginTotpStep1` key previously held a Lithuanian translation (`Įdiekite <a href="https://freeotp.github.io/"...`) and was replaced with the Italian string `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`. Surrounding `loginTotpStep2` and `loginTotpStep3` are still Lithuanian, making the file internally inconsistent. The Lithuanian translation is now lost to users. The new sanitizer does not verify language matches and therefore will not detect this regression.

English source `templateHelp` typo `<NAME >` not fixed

The English source string `templateHelp` contains `CLAIM.<NAME > ...` with a stray trailing space inside the angle brackets (`<NAME >` instead of `<NAME>`). The Chinese translation in `messages_zh_CN.properties` was corrected to `CLAIM.<NAME>`, but the English source on which all other translations are based still contains the typo. Any future translation that copies the English literally will reintroduce the typo. The verifier handles this for `templateHelp` via `normalizeValue`, but only for that specific key; the underlying source string is inconsistent with the rest of the translations.

HTML_TAGS regex is too restrictive for HTML detection

`HTML_TAGS` is defined as `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")`. This only matches tags whose first character after `<` is a lowercase ASCII letter, so `<DIV>`, `<H1>`, `<h1>`, `<a1>` and any tag name containing a digit or uppercase letter will not be detected. The OWASP sanitizer is case-insensitive and HTML spec tags are case-insensitive, so this leads to false negatives in `containsHtml()` and inconsistent classification between POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML. In practice this can produce false positives (e.g. English `<H1>` falls through to POLICY_NO_HTML, the sanitizer strips the tag, and the verifier reports `Illegal HTML` for the translation even though both sides are identical). Fix by using a case-insensitive pattern or by parsing via the sanitizer itself.

verifySafeHtml throws RuntimeException, not MojoExecutionException

`verifySafeHtml()` is called from `verify()` which declares `throws MojoExecutionException`. However `verifySafeHtml()` catches `IOException` and rethrows it as `new RuntimeException(...)`. A `RuntimeException` is not caught by the surrounding `catch (IOException e)` block in `verify()`, so it propagates unchecked and aborts the build with an unhandled exception instead of being wrapped into a `MojoExecutionException` with the existing error formatting. Either rethrow as `MojoExecutionException` (and declare it) or add the message to the `messages` list so the build produces a useful diagnostic.

Limited test coverage of HTML sanitizer behavior

The added tests cover only the simplest cases: duplicate keys, illegal HTML tag, HTML where the English has none, and changed anchor URL. They do not cover: (1) the legitimate-translation case where English has HTML and target has the same HTML (which should pass); (2) case-insensitive HTML in the English source; (3) HTML-like placeholders such as `<NAME>` or `<USERNAME>` in messages that are not whitelisted in `normalizeValue`; (4) multiple anchors; (5) anchors that differ only in inner text but keep the same URL (legitimate translations of link text); (6) `errorTitleHtml`-style keys where the English contains `<strong>` and the translation must keep it. Adding these tests would catch regressions in the sanitizer logic and the normalization rules.

normalizeValue special-cases only a few keys, risking false positives

`normalizeValue` strips HTML-looking content only for `templateHelp`, `optimizeLookupHelp`, `linkExpirationFormatter.timePeriodUnit*`, and `error-invalid-multivalued-size`. Any other message that legitimately contains text resembling an HTML tag (e.g., `<NAME>`, `<USERNAME>`, `<EMAIL>`, or any other MessageFormat placeholder that the translator chose to write with angle brackets) will be stripped by the OWASP sanitizer under POLICY_NO_HTML and the verifier will incorrectly report `Illegal HTML`. For example, any key like `fooBarTemplate=Hello <NAME>` will fail verification because `<NAME>` is not an allowed tag. Either broaden the placeholder normalization or detect via the sanitizer whether the English contains any disallowed HTML before applying POLICY_NO_HTML (i.e., compare normalized values against sanitized English, not against the raw translation).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste error in requireNonNull message

Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") reuses the previous line's check on grantType and labels the message as if it were for rawTokenId. The intended line is almost certainly Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed"). With this typo, if a caller passes a null rawTokenId, the failure message says "Null rawTokenId not allowed" but does so from the grantType check, while the rawTokenId is never validated at all and is allowed to be null.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the requireNonNull call checks grantType a second time instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId is never validated.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher does not actually verify the expected grant type

In the new isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut) matcher: (a) the condition is inverted ('return false' when the substring equals the expected grant), and (b) the offset is wrong. The token id format produced by encodeTokenId is ST(2) + TT(2) + GT(2) + ':' + rawId, so the grant shortcut occupies characters at 0-indexed positions 4 and 5 (substring(4,6)). The matcher uses substring(3,5), which is the last char of the token type and the first char of the grant type ("ta" for the example in the PR description, "ac" would actually be at substring(4,6)). Because of the offset, the substring will never equal the expected grant, and because of the inversion the branch returns false instead of true even if it did. As a result, every call site that now uses isAccessTokenId(...) (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) effectively only checks that the token id has the form 'XXXXXX:UUID' and does not actually verify the grant type. The whole point of these test changes - to detect wrong grant shortcut mapping after this PR - is silently lost.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same two problems as the golden comment in isAccessTokenId. First, the substring offset is wrong: it should be substring(4,6). Second, the equality check is inverted: a match returns false instead of true.

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract method on the grant SPI breaks every external implementation

Adding String getShortcut() as an abstract method on OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a binary- and source-incompatible change for every third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation (including in the many extensions Keycloak ships). Any out-of-tree impl compiled against the previous version will fail to load at runtime with AbstractMethodError and any extension maintainer will fail to compile against the new version. The field is internal SPI (server-spi-private), but it is still on an interface implemented by SPIs in extension points (Ciba, Device, TokenExchange, UMA Permission, etc.). At a minimum the new method needs a default implementation (e.g. default returning getId()) and the existing built-in factories should override it.

Removed public Context copy constructor

The diff removes the public Context(Context context) copy constructor from OAuth2GrantType.Context (the rest of the constructors remain). Even for 'internal' SPI in the server-spi-private module, this is a binary-incompatible removal: existing compiled callsites and any extension using that constructor will fail with NoSuchMethodError at runtime. If a copy constructor was no longer needed, that should be confirmed; if it was, it should be retained.

getShouldUseLightweightToken promoted from package-private instance to public static

The method signature was changed from 'boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(KeycloakSession session)' (package-private instance) to 'public static boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(KeycloakSession session)'. Subclasses outside this package that overrode the package-private instance version will now have two distinct methods (the inherited one and their override) and call sites using their subclass reference would still hit the parent's version. It would be safer to keep an instance-method shim (e.g. protected boolean getShouldUseLightweightToken(...) that delegates to a public static) so that subclasses continue to work, or document and version the change explicitly.

Duplicated-grant-shortcut validation fires after entries already overwritten, error message misleading

In postInit the loop does grantsByShortcuts.put(grantShortcut, grantName) for each grant. If two factories return the same shortcut, the later entry silently overwrites the earlier one in grantsByShortcuts, but grantsToShortcuts still contains both grant ids. The only validation is the post-loop size check, which catches it but the exception message just says 'Make sure there is no OAuth2GrantType implementation with same ID or shortcut like other grants' and does not identify which shortcut collided. The same race exists in getShortcutByGrantType (lazy refresh path), which does grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType) and grantsToShortcuts.put(grantType, shortcut) without any uniqueness check on the shortcut. If a misbehaving third-party provider returns a shortcut that collides with an existing one, this will silently corrupt the cached mapping at runtime.

Constants.GRANT_TYPE is only set on the refresh path, not consistently on all token-issuance paths

The grant-type attribute is set in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse, ResourceOwnerPasswordCredentialsGrantType.process, StandardTokenExchangeProvider.exchangeClientToOIDCClient, PreAuthorizedCodeGrantType.process, and (for refresh) TokenManager.validateToken. Any future caller of TokenManager.createClientAccessToken / initToken that does not first call one of these will silently fall back to the 'na' (unknown) shortcut in the encoded JTI. Constants.GRANT_TYPE is documented as the canonical key, but the responsibility for populating it is spread across many call sites with no guard. This should either be enforced inside createClientAccessToken/initToken (refuse to issue without a known grant type) or documented; otherwise the encoding will appear to work yet the encoded grant type will be 'na' for missed paths.

getTokenContextFromTokenId will NPE on null input and does not validate token id length when no colon

getTokenContextFromTokenId(encodedTokenId) calls encodedTokenId.indexOf(':') without a null check. If it is called with a null token id (e.g. a token whose jti claim ended up null/unset, which is possible when no raw id was supplied), it will throw NullPointerException instead of returning the UNKNOWN context. Also, the decoder accepts 'no colon' strings of any length (including empty string) and treats the whole input as the raw id, which means a malformed token id that contains a colon later in the string (rather than as separator) could be parsed incorrectly because indexOf only finds the first ':'.

OAuth2GrantType.Context.grantType is captured at construction time but setFormParams can replace the params later

The new grantType field is initialized once in the constructor from formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE), but the class still exposes setFormParams(...) which replaces the entire formParams map without updating grantType. Any flow that calls setFormParams after construction (the existence of that setter suggests it happens) will leave grantType pointing at the original form value, while getFormParams() returns the new one. The downstream constant Constants.GRANT_TYPE will then be the stale value, and the encoded JTI will carry the wrong grant shortcut.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean crashes if user has no recovery codes

The constructor does `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(credentialModelOpt.get())` directly on the result of `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)`, which returns `Optional<CredentialModel>`. If the user has never configured recovery codes (e.g. the bean is rendered for a user in any context where they don't exist), `get()` throws `java.util.NoSuchElementException` and the login template fails to render. This was safe before the change because the previous code used `findFirst().get()` on the local-credentials stream and would throw a similar error, but the new code now also considers federated credentials and the same fragility remains; an explicit `isPresent()` check (and a sensible fallback when absent) is required.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to calling Optional.get() on RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without an isPresent() check, which can throw NoSuchElementException. The candidate does not mention the raw List deserialization part of the golden comment, but the core Optional.get() issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCredentials returns a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel with a regenerated id

`getCredentials` constructs the returned `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` via `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(rawCodes, createdDate, userLabel)`, which does not take the existing `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()`. Every time the credential is listed, a new id is generated. Downstream consumers that try to manage the credential by id — including the new `removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())` in `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` — then operate on a non-existent local-storage id, so any per-id operation (remove, update, disable) against the federated credential silently no-ops. `getCredentials` should return a model whose `getId()` equals `myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same problem: the created RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel does not carry the stored credential id (myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()), so removeStoredCredentialById fails downstream. The candidate says a new id is regenerated where the golden says it would be null, but the bug and the fix are the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated recovery-codes credential never removed when all codes are used

When a user has recovery codes stored in federated storage and all codes have been consumed, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. `removeStoredCredentialById` only acts on credentials in local Keycloak storage, not on federated credentials returned via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. The result is that the (now exhausted) credential remains in the user storage and is still picked up by `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` on subsequent logins, so the user is repeatedly asked to re-configure while the stale credential is never cleaned up. There must be a separate path (or a fallback to a federated-credential delete) when the credential was returned from the user storage.

Recovery codes stored and compared in plaintext in user storage

`updateCredential` stores `input.getChallengeResponse()` (the raw codes JSON) directly in `credentialData`, and `isValid` reads it back and does `generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`. Recovery codes are intended to be one-time, low-trust-secret recovery material and the local Keycloak provider stores them hashed (via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode`). Storing them as plaintext and comparing raw-vs-raw in the user-storage SPI means a breach of this user storage yields every still-valid recovery code in cleartext, and provides a copy-paste template that propagates this insecure pattern to real user-storage implementations. The `isValid` path should normalize through the same hash used by the local provider, and the stored credential data should be hashed at rest.

New recovery-codes integration test covers only one happy path

`testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` exercises exactly one successful login with the first requested recovery code. It does not cover: (a) reusing the same code a second time (must fail), (b) entering an invalid code (must fail with the configured error), (c) using every code in sequence until `allCodesUsed()` triggers the required action and removes the credential (the path the diff actually changed), or (d) disabling the recovery-codes credential via the admin REST. The cleanup/id-mismatch bug noted above would not be caught by this test because the all-codes-used branch is never reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Breaking change: recreate-upgrade exit code changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was changed from 4 to 3 to free up exit code 4 for the new FEATURE_DISABLED case. This silently changes the public CLI contract of `kc.sh update-compatibility check` for any existing user. Pipelines/scripts that detect a required recreate upgrade by checking `if [ $? -eq 4 ]` will no longer match and will incorrectly conclude the deployment succeeded or that the feature was disabled. Because the PR description does not call this out as a breaking change and the docs are updated as if the new mapping was always in effect, users upgrading will be broken without warning. The change should either be reverted (keep 4 for recreate and pick another code for FEATURE_DISABLED, e.g. 5) or prominently documented as a breaking change in the release notes.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment asks for changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change. The candidate flags the same exit code change as breaking and recommends documenting it prominently in the release notes. Both point to the same concern.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for `update-compatibility check` when the rolling-updates feature is disabled

The new `testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises `update-compatibility metadata` without enabling the feature. The matching code path in `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` that prints `printFeatureDisabled()` and exits with `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` (=4) is left uncovered. A symmetric test such as `@Launch({UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityCheck.NAME})` asserting the same error message would lock in the contract for both subcommands and prevent one of them silently regressing.

The CAUTION says "While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail." This is misleading: the operator still functions with the default (legacy) update strategy when the feature is not enabled, as demonstrated by `UpgradeTest.createInitialDeployment` whose `updateStrategy == null` branch returns the Keycloak CR without enabling the feature and the test still passes. The wording should clarify that the feature is only required when the user sets `spec.update.strategy`; otherwise readers may believe enabling rolling-updates is mandatory for any Keycloak deployment.

CAUTION removed the prior TODO without leaving context for readers

The diff replaces a one-line `// TODO Link to discussion?` comment with a CAUTION block. While the new CAUTION is informative, it does not link to or mention the discussion referenced by `previewDiscussionLink` (keycloak/keycloak#36785), even though the discussion is the canonical place for users to give feedback while the command is preview. Either keep a pointer to the discussion or rely on `previewDiscussionLink` already being rendered at the top of the page, but ensure the CAUTION does not inadvertently hide the feedback channel from users experimenting with the tool.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
registerListener gates V2-only deployments off event-driven cleanup

The new wrapper uses Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) (the legacy V1 flag), but the listener body delegates to management(...) which dispatches on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 and can return MgmtPermissionsV2. When a realm runs with only V2 enabled and V1 disabled, the entire listener body is now skipped, so ClientRemovedEvent, RoleRemovedEvent, and GroupRemovedEvent will not trigger any cleanup of the V2 resources/scopes/policies those objects back. The check needs to consider ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 (either in addition to or instead of the V1 flag) so that pure-V2 realms still receive the event-driven cleanup.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The listener is gated on the V1 ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ flag, so when only V2 is enabled, cleanup on role, client, or group removal is skipped and permissions are left orphaned.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission includes the "Clients" all-resource name in result set

resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) iterates over every resource of type "Clients", which includes both per-client resources (named client.getId()) and the all-clients resource created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init() with the name "Clients". When the caller holds an all-clients scope permission, hasGrantedPermission returns true for that all-clients resource and the literal string "Clients" is added to the returned set alongside any real client UUIDs. Callers using this set to filter or load clients will misinterpret the resource-type string as a client ID (lookups will fail) and the absence of a distinct "all" indicator means the all-clients case is silently lost. The loop must either skip the all-clients resource (compare resource.getName() to AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) or model the all-clients case as a separate sentinel.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say getClientsWithPermission returns the type-level 'Clients' resource name, not real client IDs, so client lookups by ID fail. They differ on whether per-client resources are also returned, but the core bug is the same: the 'Clients' name is treated as a client ID.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission(ClientModel, String) can NPE when all-clients resource is missing

When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the all-clients resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...). If the schema resource server has not been initialized (or the resource was otherwise removed), getResourceTypeResource returns null, and the subsequent authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) is invoked with a null resource and throws a NullPointerException. This path is reached on every per-client permission check when no all-clients policy has been created yet, so it is reachable in production during early realm setup. Add a null check on the resource returned from getResourceTypeResource before calling findByResource.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug in hasPermission. getResourceTypeResource can return null, which leads to an NPE in findByResource. Both recommend a null check before that call.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadocs on several interface methods omit V2 behavior notes

Methods such as canList(), requireList(), canViewClientScopes(), requireViewClientScopes(), canListClientScopes(), requireListClientScopes(), and requireView() are newly documented in this PR but, unlike canManage/canView/canView(ClientModel)/canConfigure(ClientModel)/canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles, do not include the "For V2 only: ..." clause that explains the FGAP fallback used by ClientPermissionsV2. Because ClientPermissionsV2 does not override any of these (canList/canViewClientScopes/canListClientScopes all fall through to the V1 implementation), readers cannot tell how these methods behave under ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Add the missing "For V2 only" notes (or note explicitly that they inherit V1 behavior unchanged) so the contract is clear.

No integration test for VIEW-per-client or all-clients CONFIGURE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE in V2

PermissionClientTest adds coverage for MANAGE per-client (testManageOnlyOneClient), CONFIGURE per-client (testConfigureOnlyOneClient), MANAGE all-clients (testManageAllClients), VIEW all-clients (testViewAllClients), and MAP_ROLES+MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE per-client (testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient). It never exercises VIEW scoped to a single client, CONFIGURE granted on the all-clients resource, or MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE at all. Since ClientPermissionsV2.canView(ClientModel), canConfigure(ClientModel) (all-clients branch in hasPermission) and canMapClientScopeRoles(ClientModel) are brand new code paths, at least one positive and one negative test for each is needed to lock in behavior; without them, regressions in those branches (for example the "Clients" leak in getClientsWithPermission, or the NPE in hasPermission) will not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission only sees the all-groups resource, ignoring individual group permissions

The implementation iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, …)`, but `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource` never sets the resource type on the per-entity resources it creates (see AdminPermissionsSchema.java around line 121), so `findByType("Groups", …)` returns only the synthetic all-groups resource created during `init()`. In addition the lambda calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), …)` (a UUID produced by the resource store) while `hasPermission` resolves resources by `findByName` against the group UUID, and then `granted.add(groupResource.getId())` adds the resource UUID into a set that callers (UsersResource.searchForUser and BruteForceUsersResource.searchForUser) treat as group IDs to populate `UserModel.GROUPS`. The net effect is that group-specific VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions are completely ignored; only a permission on the all-groups resource can populate the set. As a consequence, an admin whose only permissions are scoped to a specific group will not be filtered to members of that group when listing users, and the new test `testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers` cannot pass under FGAP V2.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same mismatch the golden comment describes. hasPermission is called with the resource ID while it resolves resources by name (group id), and the resource ID is added to a set used as group IDs. As a result, only the all-groups resource is effectively evaluated. The candidate adds a point about findByType, but the core issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE potential when all-groups resource lookup returns null

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, when the per-group lookup fails the code calls `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE);` and on the next line dereferences it directly with `if (policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty())`. getResourceTypeResource can return null when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false or when the synthetic all-groups resource has not been created. The missing null check will throw NullPointerException on the first FGAP V2 group-evaluation call that hits this path. The guard must be `resource == null || policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()` (or equivalent) before evaluating permissions.

Same NPE pattern in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission fallback

UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission assigns `resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, AdminPermissionsSchema.USERS_RESOURCE_TYPE);` and immediately dereferences it on the next line in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty()`. If the all-users resource does not exist (e.g., schema not yet initialised) this throws NullPointerException, breaking V2 per-user evaluations (canView/canManage/canMapRoles/canImpersonate/canManageGroupMembership on a specific user). A null guard before the policy lookup is required.

Individually-created resources are not tagged with their resource type

`TotalDocs` does `for _, v := range b.cache { ... }` with no lock acquisition, while `BuildIndex` (now able to run concurrently with other builds and with any caller of `TotalDocs`) writes to `b.cache` under `b.cacheMu`. Iterating a Go map while it is being written to is a data race and is documented as able to panic with "fatal error: concurrent map read and map write" or "concurrent map writes". `TotalDocs` is part of the `SearchBackend` interface and is called from `searchSupport.init` via `s.search.TotalDocs()` immediately after `group.Wait()`, but it may also be invoked from elsewhere (metrics endpoints, future callers). It should at least take `b.cacheMu.RLock()` for the duration of the iteration. Previously this was masked because the lock was held during the whole `BuildIndex`; with the finer-grained locking the race window is now larger.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without a lock while BuildIndex writes to it concurrently, which can cause a concurrent map read/write panic. Both also point to the TotalDocs call in init. The candidate attributes the concurrency less specifically to the event watcher goroutine, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Init triggers two WatchWriteEvents calls; SQL backend spawns two pollers

`(*server).Init` is now called from `NewResourceServer` and unconditionally runs both `s.search.init(ctx)` and `s.initWatcher()`. `search.init` itself calls `s.storage.WatchWriteEvents(watchctx)` and starts a long-lived goroutine that consumes from that channel. `initWatcher` then constructs a `Broadcaster` whose subscriber-setup callback also calls `s.backend.WatchWriteEvents(s.ctx)` the first time a client subscribes via `Watch`. For the SQL backend, `WatchWriteEvents` is implemented as `go b.poller(ctx, since, stream)` (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:566), so every call spins up a new poller goroutine that polls the database every 100ms. After this PR, every Grafana process with unified storage enabled runs two such pollers against the same database and reads the same history rows, doubling query load and (for `search.init`'s consumer) processing events from a completely separate stream than the `Broadcaster`. The PR explicitly reorders the init code but does not address this; the right fix is to have `search.init` subscribe to the existing `Broadcaster` instead of opening a second watcher. This was pre-existing but is directly within the scope of the init restructuring and should be resolved in the same change.

NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build and leaks partial state on Init failure

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` if it fails. There are three consequences a maintainer should be aware of: (1) every caller of the constructor now blocks for as long as it takes to build every search index, which is a contract change from the previous "return fast, build on first gRPC call" behavior; this can affect test fixtures, alternate startup paths, and any code that constructs a `ResourceServer` and expects immediate return. (2) If `search.init` fails partway through, indexes that were successfully built remain in the bleve cache and any partially-started watcher goroutine is not torn down, because `Stop` is not called when returning `(nil, err)`. (3) The internal `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` pair is created on the success path of construction but on the failure path the `cancel` function (held in `s.cancel`) is never invoked and the context has no parent cancellation. The constructor should either run init with a `defer cancel()` so failure cleans up, or document the new contract explicitly. Note also that `pkg/server/module_server_test.go` now skips postgres for the storage server target — likely a symptom of this new blocking init interacting with the test harness, which suggests the contract change is observable from outside the unified storage package.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of its docstring intent and fails

The test docstring says 'errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the final assertion is `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which is the opposite. With the current implementation (`OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `Exception`, logs it, and in `finally` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`), both messages get their offsets marked complete regardless of the raised exception. The commit loop then commits offset 101 → Kafka offset 102. So `committed_offsets` will be `{test_partition: 102}`, both halves of the disjunction are False, and the test fails. The assertion should instead verify that the commit did happen (matching the docstring), e.g. `assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102`. As written, the test contradicts the implementation's actual behavior and would never pass.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say the docstring of test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling contradicts what the test actually asserts. The candidate adds more detail, but the underlying issue is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
OffsetTracker commits past unseen offsets, causing silent data loss

In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed` (lines 100–105), after committing offset X, all offsets ≤ X are removed from `self.all_offsets`. On the next `get_committable_offsets` call, the loop starts at `max(last_committed + 1, min(all_offsets))`, so any offset that was never submitted to the tracker is forgotten. If the consumer skips an offset (e.g., 101) but submits 100, 102, 103, the tracker will first commit 100 then, after removal, commit 103 — committing past the unseen 101 to Kafka. On restart, Kafka would begin reading from offset 104, permanently losing offset 101. The tracker assumes gaps are always due to filtering/compaction, but it has no way to distinguish that from a bug where `submit()` was never called for an offset. The test `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py` was clearly designed to catch this behavior (it asserts commits never exceed 101), but the implementation violates that assertion — the last commit would be 104. A safer design would either keep removed offsets to detect gaps, or require every offset in [last_committed, X] to have been at least seen.

Code depends on Python 3.13-only queue APIs

The file uses `queue.ShutDown` (caught in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` lines 132 and 142) and `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` in `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` (line 238). Both `queue.Queue.shutdown()` and the `queue.ShutDown` exception were introduced in Python 3.13 (October 2024). If sentry still supports Python 3.11 or 3.12, the workers will crash with `AttributeError: module 'queue' has no attribute 'ShutDown'` / `'shutdown'` the first time a shutdown is attempted or an exception is raised inside `run()`. The minimum Python version supported by sentry needs to be verified; if it is below 3.13, this module cannot be imported safely and will break the uptime-results consumer at runtime. A portable alternative is to use a sentinel object via `Queue.put` and check it in the worker, or a `threading.Event` plus a final empty marker, neither requiring Python 3.13.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.terminate does not join commit thread

`terminate` sets `shutdown_event` and calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, but unlike `close` it never calls `self.commit_thread.join(...)`. The commit thread is daemonized, so the process exit will reap it, but during the window between `terminate` returning and the process actually exiting, the commit thread can still invoke `self.commit_function` (the arroyo `commit` callback) and mutate `OffsetTracker` state. This violates the symmetry with `close`, and means callers using `terminate` for a forced shutdown can have an arbitrary amount of background work still running against a strategy they consider terminated.

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores its timeout argument

`join(self, timeout: float | None = None)` simply calls `self.close()`, dropping the `timeout` parameter. `close()` in turn calls `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` (hard-coded 5s) and `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (which joins workers with another hard-coded 5s). Callers that pass a smaller timeout via `join(0.5)` expecting bounded shutdown will wait up to ~10 seconds instead. The `timeout` argument should either be honored by passing it to the underlying joins or removed from the signature.

test_different_groups_distributed is probabilistic and can be flaky

The test submits 20 distinct group keys to a pool of 3 queues and asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3`. The probability of missing a queue with 20 keys and 3 buckets is 3 * (2/3)^20 - 3 * (1/3)^20 ≈ 0.00078, or about 1 in 1300. With Python's randomized string hashing (`PYTHONHASHSEED`) this is not controllable from the test. Worse, `hash()` can in principle produce collisions that bunch keys into fewer buckets than expected. The test should either use enough keys that the probability of collision is negligible (e.g. 200+), or directly assert `>= 2` rather than `== 3`, or seed/force the hash distribution.

Kafka integration test relies on private methods and tight timing

`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest.test_thread_queue_parallel_kafka_offset_commit` reaches into `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()` (private Arroyo APIs) and only spins for 5 seconds before asserting `committed[0].offset == 5`. Under load or slow CI the consumer may not have time to fetch, decode, queue, and commit all 5 messages; the assertion then fails for timing reasons rather than correctness. Additionally, the test wraps `factory.create_with_partitions` to count commits but does not verify that all produced messages were actually decoded (`mock_processor.return_value = None` bypasses real processing). Consider using Arroyo's public `run()` loop, increasing the deadline, and asserting a lower bound (e.g. offset >= 1) rather than equality.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator negative slicing will raise AssertionError

The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with `start_offset = cursor.offset` (a negative integer) when `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`. Django QuerySets explicitly do not support negative indexing; `QuerySet.__getitem__` asserts `int(k.start) >= 0` and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The inline comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. Any admin-supplied cursor string like `"0:-10:0"` (Cursor.from_string parses the second token via `int(bits[1])`) will crash the endpoint with a 500. This also contradicts the docstring claim that the feature is "safe" — it is not even reachable without a server error. Either remove the negative-offset branch or fetch a count first and translate the offset to a positive LIMIT/OFFSET in SQL.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch passes cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True. The candidate adds detail on the resulting crash (Django rejects negative indexing), but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
KeyError on spans missing end_timestamp_precise

The new code uses `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with subscript access, while every other optional field in the same Span constructor (parent_span_id, is_remote) uses `.get()`. Any span payload already buffered in the ingest-spans Kafka topic (or coming from a producer that has not yet been upgraded) that lacks this key will raise KeyError and crash the consumer batch. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` (or fall back to a sentinel such as 0.0) for forward compatibility with in-flight messages.

max_segment_spans protection silently removed from flush path

`_load_segment_data` previously guarded against runaway segments by deleting any key whose accumulated span count exceeded `self.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) and emitting the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric. The diff deletes that branch entirely and the constructor parameter `max_segment_spans` is now dead — no code reads it. The new in-Lua `zpopmin` eviction runs on the insert path, but it does not protect against (a) segments populated before this rollout, (b) sets that exceed 1000 entries between two insert calls, or (c) the case where `zcard(set_key)` after `zunionstore` returns 0 because both source sets were empty (so eviction is skipped even though `zcard` afterward would still report >1000). Without the flush-time guard a single oversized segment will now be loaded into memory and serialized, which is exactly what the old check prevented.

zpopmin eviction key is not actually oldest spans

Eviction uses `zpopmin` against `end_timestamp_precise` scores. When many spans in a segment share the same `end_timestamp_precise` (which is the common case for spans belonging to the same transaction), Redis sorted-set ordering for ties is lexicographic on the member bytes, i.e. on the JSON payload. The "evict oldest" policy therefore degenerates to "evict whichever serialized payload sorts first," which is essentially arbitrary and may preferentially drop small/different payloads. The score should include a deterministic tiebreaker (e.g. span_id) so eviction order is reproducible.

OptimizedCursorPaginator added with no test coverage

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result with a security-relevant behavior change (allowing negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features=True`). It is wired into the audit-logs endpoint and gated only by `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but there are zero tests for the class itself, for `enable_advanced_features=True` path, for negative offsets, or for the auditlog endpoint's new `optimized_pagination=true` branch. A paginator that silently changes the cursor contract for admins deserves its own tests in tests/sentry/api/test_paginator.py and tests/sentry/api/endpoints/test_organization_auditlogs.py.

Pre-existing typo order_b still present in BasePaginator.build_queryset

In `BasePaginator.build_queryset` the branch that flips `-key` ordering back to ascending writes `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` — `order_b` is not an attribute of `Query` (the correct attribute is `order_by`). As a result, the reversed ordering is silently dropped and the queryset is left ordered by `-key` even though the code intended `+key`. This is in the same file the diff touches and is exercised by every caller using a descending order_by with a `is_prev=True` cursor that has a cursor value. It must be fixed before this PR lands; the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` inherits from `BasePaginator` and inherits the bug.

Endpoint change misrepresented as performance optimization

The endpoint change is labeled "Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns" and the new query parameter is named `optimized_pagination`, but `OptimizedCursorPaginator` produces the same SQL plan as `DateTimePaginator` for the normal (forward, non-negative offset) case; the only functional difference is that it permits negative cursor offsets. There is no benchmark, no documentation in `api-docs/` (Sentry typically gates new query params), and no mention that the new branch is only active for superusers/org members with global access — `enable_advanced_features=True` is silently enabled based on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, which is not the same permission check used elsewhere in this endpoint (`OrganizationAuditPermission`). Either rename the parameter to reflect what it actually does (e.g. `allow_negative_offset`) and document it, or drop the class.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key uses hash() of project_ids tuple

The cache key is built as `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. While `hash(int)` is deterministic in CPython, mixing `hash()` of a derived structure into a cache key is fragile (it depends on tuple-hash internals and any future changes to them) and produces opaque keys that are hard to inspect/grep in Redis. A deterministic, explicit key like `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))}"` (or a sha1 prefix) would be safer, debuggable, and immune to future interpreter changes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same code: hash() used in the cache key, with the same fix of deterministic serialization. The candidate's justification differs. It explicitly says hash(int) is deterministic, which is true because hash randomization applies only to str and bytes. It calls the approach fragile rather than non-deterministic across processes. The location and fix are the same, and both see a determinism risk, so this largely counts as the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count SnQLFunction not marked private

The newly added `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, unlike the surrounding private helpers (e.g. `thing_expression`, `count_at_least`). Without that flag the function becomes part of the user-exposed SnQL/Discover function surface, so end users could write `upsampled_count()` in their own queries. The function is only meaningful in conjunction with the project allowlist/sampling-rate pipeline, and emits `sum(sample_weight)` which has different semantics (and potential NULL-handling) from `count()`. Users invoking it directly outside of `organization_events_stats` will get counts that silently diverge from what they expect.

sum(sample_weight) silently drops NULL sample_weight rows

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count()` which is implemented as `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. ClickHouse/SnQL `sum` ignores NULL arguments entirely, so any allowlisted-project event that has `sample_weight IS NULL` is silently omitted from the result, undercounting errors. The comment claims the schema guarantees `sample_weight` is non-null for allowlisted projects, but nothing in this helper (or in `discover.py`) enforces or even validates that invariant. There should be at minimum a guard that rejects the transformation (or coalesces `sample_weight` to a fallback) when the project list could contain NULL-weight events, otherwise dashboards/alerts that switch to upsampled counts will report numbers lower than the truth with no warning.

transform only matches literal count(), misses aliased and surrounded variants

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` compares `column.lower().strip() == "count()"`. This single-equality test misses common variants that should still be upsampled: `count() as my_count`, `count() AS errors`, `count("id")` (counting a specific column), or `count()` surrounded by extra inner whitespace. As a result, a column written as `count() as count` (with explicit alias) will be passed through unchanged while the same column written as `count()` will be replaced with `upsampled_count() as count`, giving two clients querying the same metric different aggregations. The transform should at least recognise `count()` with a trailing `as <alias>` clause.

_is_error_focused_query uses substring match on query string

`_is_error_focused_query` decides based on `"event.type:error" in query`. The check is a raw substring match, so queries like `event.type:error_handled` (if such an alias is ever introduced) or any token that begins with `event.type:error` would be treated as error-focused and force the upsampled transformation on a dataset that may include non-error rows. A safer check parses the query tokens (e.g. via `event_search.parse_search_query`) and inspects the actual `event.type` value rather than doing a substring `in`.

Error message wording regression adjacent to top_events validation

The diff changes the response message from `"If topEvents needs to be at least 1"` to `"topEvents needs to be at least 1"`. The new wording is grammatically cleaner, but it is bundled into a commit titled `feat(upsampling)` with no mention of an API/UX message change. Because this is a public 400 response body on `organization-events-stats`, any client that does an exact-string match on this `detail` value (e.g. localised tooling) will break. The change should either be split into its own commit or called out in the description.

Unnecessary try/except around safe dict lookups

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps the chained `.get(...).get(...).get(...)` in a `try/except Exception: pass` and the `float(...)` conversion in another one. `dict.get` cannot raise for missing keys, and a malformed `client_sample_rate` string is the only realistic failure mode, which the second `try` already handles. The first try/except hides real bugs (e.g. `AttributeError` from a malformed contexts payload) and should be removed; only the `float()` conversion needs to be defensive.

setUp reassigns self.user after login_as, breaking auth identity

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, the test calls `self.login_as(user=self.user)` with the user that `APITestCase.setUp` created, then immediately overwrites `self.user = self.create_user()`. From that point on, `self.user` no longer refers to the authenticated user, and any tag, audit log entry, or future test that reads `self.user` will silently use the wrong identity. In particular the events stored right below use `self.user.email` / `self.user2.email` as the `sentry:user` tag, which means the test is asserting counts against events whose owner does not match the calling API user; if any later assertion (or downstream test) compares user identity this will fail.

Stale upsampling eligibility cache has no invalidation hook

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches the all-projects-in-allowlist result for 60 seconds, and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is provided but never called from anywhere in the diff (no admin signal, option listener, or tests cover invalidation). entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()
defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()
if entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev {
    return entryPointAssetsCache, nil
}

In deleteByIDs, when running on SQLite with a batch size > 999, the code builds the IN-list by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf('%s, %d', values, v) inside a loop. Each iteration allocates a new string of length O(i), giving O(n^2) work and O(n^2) intermediate allocations. For a batch of 32767 IDs this is on the order of a billion character copies. Use strings.Builder or a single fmt.Sprintf with a precomputed separator, or strings.Join over strconv formatted values. The new integration test exercises exactly this path with 32767 IDs, so the cost will show up in CI and any production SQLite deployment configured with a large batch size.

deleteByIDs switches to the inlined-SQL branch when r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit. The branch should depend on len(ids), not on the configured batch size: if the operator has set a large batch size but a particular batch returns only a handful of ids (common when there are few rows left to clean), we still go down the inlined-SQL path and pay the O(n^2) cost for no benefit. Conversely, if the operator mis-configures AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize to be small (<= 999) while the actual returned ids somehow exceed that (e.g. via a future change), we would silently use the parameterized path and potentially exceed SQLite's parameter limit. Use len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit as the gate.

A concurrent transaction can insert new annotations that satisfy the same cleanup predicate (MaxAge cutoff or MaxCount offset) between fetch and delete; those new rows will not be in the fetched id set and so will not be deleted this cycle. The author documented this as 'may under-delete... any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle', which is acceptable, but the test suite does not exercise this scenario (no concurrent inserter) and there is no log/instrumentation that would let an operator detect persistent under-deletion. The new code interpolates every query via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before `partition(...)` runs `querySupportsSplitting`, which relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to exclude queries whose `$__range` would be interpolated on the backend with the split time range. The split sub-requests are then dispatched with the full-range literal inside the expression but a per-chunk time range, so each sub-query computes its rate over the wrong window and the merged result is incorrect. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race lets device count exceed the configured limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then either updateDevice or an INSERT as two separate, non-atomic steps (lines 109-118 and the switch/INSERT at 120-153). Under concurrent anonymous authentications many goroutines can each observe count < deviceLimit, all proceed to insert, and the resulting count can exceed deviceLimit by the concurrency level. This defeats the stated purpose of the feature — the limit is not a hard cap but only an approximate one, and a burst of legitimate users (or a small attacker) can inflate the table well past it. Wrap the check and write in a single transaction (or use a serializable isolation level / advisory lock) so the limit is enforced atomically.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same race condition. Concurrent requests can pass the device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both suggest a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice uses device.UpdatedAt as its time reference while CreateOrUpdateDevice uses time.Now()

In CreateOrUpdateDevice the 30-day window is built from time.Now().UTC() (line 110), but in updateDevice the WHERE bounds on updated_at are built from device.UpdatedAt.UTC() (lines 80-81). They happen to coincide today because TagDevice constructs the Device with UpdatedAt: time.Now() (impl.go line 141), but the two functions now disagree on what 'now' is. If a future caller passes a Device whose UpdatedAt is anything other than time.Now() (a replay, a clock-skew tolerance, a test fixture, a backfill, or simply a refactor), the updateDevice bounds will silently drift relative to the count window: a device that should be considered 'recent' by CreateOrUpdateDevice can be excluded by updateDevice and vice versa. Capture time.Now() once at the start of CreateOrUpdateDevice and pass it (or device.UpdatedAt derived from it) into updateDevice explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out that updateDevice uses device.UpdatedAt as the time reference for the window bounds, while time.Now().UTC() is used elsewhere. Both recommend using time.Now() consistently. This is the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit bypassed on retry via local cache

In tagDeviceUI the local cache entry is set on line 87 with a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{}) BEFORE the CreateOrUpdateDevice DB call. When the device limit is reached and that DB call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry is already populated. Any subsequent request from the same client within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the cache (line 83), returns nil immediately, and Authenticate proceeds — bypassing the limit entirely. The limit is therefore only enforced on the very first request for a given device ID; a single retry lets the user through. To actually enforce it, the cache must only be populated after a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice (or the cache key must encode the limit-reached state). This regression is introduced by the new ErrDeviceLimitReached path: the cache pattern was harmless before because all errors were swallowed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug. In tagDeviceUI the cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, so when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned the entry stays populated and later requests bypass the limit for the 29-minute TTL.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now blocks synchronously on TagDevice DB writes

Previously TagDevice was called in a goroutine with a 2-minute context timeout, so Anonymous.Authenticate returned after one DB lookup (orgService.GetByName). The new code calls TagDevice synchronously at line 44, which internally runs CountDevices (SELECT COUNT(*)) plus an INSERT/UPDATE on anon_device on every anonymous request. Each anonymous authentication now performs 2-3 DB operations instead of 1, and any DB latency or contention is added to auth latency. For Grafana instances that expose anonymous dashboards to high traffic this is a serious performance and reliability regression. The async pattern should be kept; the limit decision can be propagated via a channel, or the CountDevices check alone can be made synchronous while the write stays async.

Device-limit failure surfaces as a bare sentinel error with no HTTP semantics

Anonymous.Authenticate returns the raw sentinel var ErrDeviceLimitReached = fmt.Errorf("device limit reached") (defined in anonstore/database.go line 18) at line 46, with no HTTP status code, no machine-readable code, and no user-facing message. The authn framework will propagate this as a generic authentication failure, almost certainly a 500/Internal-Server-Error-like response to the browser. Operators have no signal that the limit is the cause (they will see only generic auth-failure logs), and end users see no indication that they are hitting a configured cap versus a real outage. Wrap the sentinel in a typed error that carries a 429/503 status and a clear message, or convert it in the HTTP layer so the response makes the cause actionable.

No test exercises the allowed update path of updateDevice at the limit

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device ID is rejected when the count has reached the limit. The crucial opposite case — a known device ID re-tags while the limit is reached and must be updated successfully via updateDevice — is not tested. This is the only path that uses updateDevice at all in this PR, and a regression that always returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (e.g., the WHERE bounds drifting to exclude every row, as flagged separately) would not be caught. Add a case with deviceLimit=1 that inserts device X, then calls CreateOrUpdateDevice with the same X again (optionally with a slightly different client_ip/user_agent) and asserts no error and that the row was actually updated.

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes sqlStore db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore (impl.go line 36), and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a new deviceLimit int64 parameter (anonstore/database.go line 52). The PR updates every direct caller it shows (impl.go and the *_test.go files) but does not include the wire-generated file(s) (e.g. wire_gen.go / providers.go / inject.go) that Grafana's wire setup regenerates from these provider signatures. Until those are regenerated the build will fail because the old ProvideAnonDBStore(store) and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService(..., anonStore, ...) calls no longer exist. Confirm the wire file is regenerated (or hand-updated) as part of this change; if it is intentionally omitted, the PR description should say so.

New auth.anonymous device_limit setting is not documented

setting.go adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0) under [auth.anonymous] at line 1650, but no documentation file is changed. The PR description itself leaves the 'docs are updated' checklist item unchecked. Operators have no reference for the new key, its default of 0 (= no limit), or its semantics (when the limit is reached, new anonymous device IDs are rejected while known devices can still re-tag). Add the key to the appropriate configuration reference (e.g. docs/sources/administration/configuration.md) and, if this is a notable improvement, link it from the What's New doc per the PR template.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
ensure_loaded! has a data race on @loaded_locales

ensure_loaded! initializes @loaded_locales ||= [] outside any mutex and then calls load_locale, which itself protects only the body via LOAD_MUTEX. Two threads that race on the first call can each observe @loaded_locales as nil, create separate Array instances, and the last write wins. Whichever instance is no longer referenced loses its additions, so subsequent calls into ensure_loaded!/load_locale can re-load already-loaded locales. The mutex currently held only by load_locale is not sufficient because @loaded_locales may flip between two arrays mid-flight. Initialize the ivar under the same LOAD_MUTEX (or use a Set guarded by the mutex) so the @loaded_locales reference itself is stable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: @loaded_locales is lazily initialized (||= []) and accessed by concurrent threads without synchronization, which causes a race.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fallback chain mixes String and Symbol locales

set_locale in application_controller.rb assigns I18n.locale from current_user.effective_locale or SiteSetting.default_locale, which return String values in Discourse. The fallback chain is [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en], so the chain can contain a String like 'fr' alongside Symbols :en. Array#uniq does not deduplicate values of different types, so 'en' and :en would both end up in the chain and load_locale would add both to @loaded_locales in translate_accelerator.rb. This results in wasted reloads and risks comparison surprises in i18n internals or third-party code. Coerce locale to a Symbol (e.g. locale.to_sym) so the chain is uniformly typed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments raise the same problem: locales passed as both String and Symbol lead to double-loading, and both recommend normalizing to a Symbol. The candidate places it in the fallback chain and load_locale, which falls under the golden comment's note that the issue applies to other locations in the PR.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new fallback behavior

The PR introduces a new FallbackLocaleList class, a custom I18n.fallbacks implementation, the new I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! method, and a new I18n.ensure_loaded! method on the freedom patch. None of these changes have accompanying specs. There is no coverage verifying: that the fallback chain order is correct for users vs anonymous requests, that I18n.locale changes between requests trigger reloads, that SiteSetting.default_locale is honored as a fallback, that missing keys in a non-English locale correctly fall back to English, or that ensure_loaded! is idempotent. The PR description 'Test 9' does not indicate tests are present anywhere.

FallbackLocaleList inherits Hash but only overrides []

FallbackLocaleList < Hash redefines only the [] method. All other methods of I18n::Locale::Fallbacks that callers may rely on (e.g. defaults, defaults=, compute, map, each over configured fallbacks, []=) are left as plain Hash methods that operate on an always-empty Hash. Any plugin or piece of code that does I18n.fallbacks[:zh_TW] = [:zh_TW, :zh_CN, :en] will silently be ignored because lookup always goes through the overridden []. Methods like I18n.fallbacks.defaults will raise NoMethodError. Either stop inheriting Hash or implement the full Locale::Fallbacks contract so that per-locale configuration and other API consumers are not broken.

ensure_loaded! allocates per request in a before_filter

set_locale runs as a before_filter on every request, and the new line invokes I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, which calls self[I18n.locale] and allocates a new Array every time, then iterates it calling I18n.ensure_loaded! for each fallback locale. The actual YAML loading is memoized via @loaded_locales, but the per-request Array allocation and Hash#[] invocation occur for every request, including API and XHR requests that never render translations. Consider calling ensure_loaded! only when the locale or SiteSetting.default_locale changes, or memoizing the resolved fallback chain on the FallbackLocaleList instance.

The PR removes config.i18n.fallbacks = true (and its explanatory comment) from config/environments/production.rb, config/environments/profile.rb, and config/cloud/cloud66/files/production.rb without leaving a comment noting that i18n fallbacks are now configured exclusively by config/initializers/i18n.rb. The two places previously disagreed in subtle ways and a future engineer may add the Rails-style line back, double-enabling the Fallbacks module, or assume the initializer is the only source of truth. Leave a one-line note in each environment file pointing at the initializer, or document the migration in the initializer itself.
